translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

This is the record of the Metropolitan Examination held in the eighteenth year of our Emperor’s Hongzhi reign, the yichou year (1505). At that time, more than 3,800 provincial graduates from throughout the realm assembled in the capital. The servants of the throne Zhang Sheng, Li Jie, and Wang Hua of the Ministry of Rites submitted a request concerning the conduct of the examination. His Majesty commanded the Hanlin Academy officials Wang Zhen and Tinghe to preside over the examination and evaluation, while Reader-in-Waiting Mao Ji and Reader-in-Waiting Xu Mu; Left Rectifier of the Heir Apparent Fu Gui; Hanlin Editors Chen Ji, Jia Yong, Liu Long, Sun Qing, Li Tingxiang, and Bi Jichuan; Chief Supervising Secretary Ren Liangbi; Supervising Secretary Zhang Hongzhi; Bureau Director Zhou Jifeng; and Secretaries Lü Yuanfu and Liu …

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
武臣則分校焉試院事一屬
之臣傑監試事一屬之御史
臣韓春臣邵蕃試士多可登
進者第選取其尤得三百人
遵
宸斷云臣元禎仰惟我
太祖高皇帝開天
===
太宗文皇帝紹統廓清夷俗載興
文治一以孔子六經正學教
育英俊而登用之蓋陋前代
詞賦之制期得振古人物以
臻隆古之化
列聖相承益懋益敷良臣碩輔班
班輩出而治效之盛前代罕
alt_text:
武臣則分校馬試院事一屬
之〔臣傑〕監試事一屬之御史
臣韓春臣邵蕃試士多可登
進者第選取其尤得三百人
遵
===
宸斷云〔臣元禎〕仰惟我
太祖高皇帝開天
太宗文皇帝紹統廓清夷俗彛典
文治一以孔子六經正學教
育英俊而登用之盖陋前代
詞賦之制期得振古人物以
臻隆古之化
列聖相承益懋益殷良臣碩輔班
班輩出而治教之盛前代罕
punctuated:
武臣則分校焉。試院事一屬之臣傑，監試事一屬之御史臣韓春、臣邵蕃。試士多可登進者，第選取其尤，得三百人，遵宸斷云。
臣元禎仰惟我太祖高皇帝開天，太宗文皇帝紹統，廓清夷俗，載興文治，一以孔子六經正學教育英俊而登用之。蓋陋前代詞賦之制，期得振古人物，以臻隆古之化。
列聖相承，益懋益敷，良臣碩輔班班輩出，而治效之盛，前代罕
translation_en:
…Liu Wuchen served among the Associate Examiners. Affairs of the examination compound were entrusted entirely to your servant Jie, and supervision of the examination entirely to the Censors, your servants Han Chun and Shao Fan. Among the candidates examined, many were worthy of advancement; selecting only the most outstanding, we obtained three hundred men, in accordance with the imperial decision.
Your servant Yuanzhen reverently reflects that our Emperor Taizu Gao founded the dynasty, and Emperor Taizong Wen succeeded to its rule. They swept away barbarian customs and renewed government through civil culture, educating outstanding men exclusively through the orthodox learning of Confucius and the Six Classics and promoting them to office. They considered inadequate the system of earlier dynasties based on literary compositions and rhapsodies, and hoped to obtain men of the stature of those of antiquity, thereby attaining the transforming influence of government in high antiquity.
The successive sage emperors carried on this legacy, ever more diligently fostering and extending it. Worthy ministers and eminent counselors emerged in conspicuous succession, and the splendid achievements of their government were seldom …

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
及顧閱世既久士狃見聞性
命之微初學或能道之而厭
常好奇駕虛競靡者又往往
是文勝質澆觀世道者慮焉
試以求哲方之前修其人品
之敦龐博大何如也其建立
之光明俊偉何如也而司校
===
取者復不能崇雅黜浮發題
多穿鑿瑣屑困以隱僻致士
益他鶩不務深植豐培馴入
仕途多干名罔實甚或蕩無
繩檢棄素學如敝屣然重惟
我
皇上臨御歲久適甲子更端於凡

===
取者復不能崇雅黜浮發題
多穿鑿瑣屑困以隱僻致士
益他騖不務深植豐培馴入
仕途多于名罔實甚哉蕩無
繩檢棄素學如敝屣䌓重惟
我
皇上臨御歲久適甲子更端於凡
punctuated:
及。顧閱世既久，士狃見聞，性命之微，初學或能道之，而厭常好奇、駕虛競靡者，又往往是。文勝質澆，觀世道者慮焉。試以求哲，方之前修，其人品之敦龐博大何如也？其建立之光明俊偉何如也？而司校取者，復不能崇雅黜浮，發題多穿鑿瑣屑，困以隱僻，致士益他鶩，不務深植豐培。馴入仕途，多干名罔實，甚或蕩無繩檢，棄素學如敝屣然。
重惟我皇上臨御歲久，適甲子更端，於凡
translation_en:
…could match. Yet, as time has passed, scholars have become habituated to what they have seen and heard. Even beginners can sometimes speak of the subtleties of human nature and destiny, while those who disdain the ordinary and delight in the strange, build upon empty notions and compete in ornate extravagance, are frequently to be found. Literary embellishment prevails, while substance grows thin: those who observe the moral condition of the age are troubled by this. Examinations serve to seek out the wise. Compared with worthy men of earlier times, how do these scholars measure up in the solidity, generosity, breadth, and greatness of their character? How do they measure up in the brilliance, uprightness, distinction, and grandeur of their accomplishments? Yet those responsible for assessing and selecting candidates also fail to uphold refinement and reject superficiality. Their questions are often forced and petty, taxing candidates with obscure and recondite matters. This causes scholars to turn increasingly to other pursuits, rather than attending to the deep rooting and ample cultivation of their learning. As they gradually enter official careers, many seek reputation without substance; some even abandon all restraint and cast aside their former learning like worn-out shoes.
We reflect with deep respect that our Emperor has occupied the throne for many years. Now, as the jiazi year marks the beginning of a new cycle, in all…

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
文武大務恢張一新況茲掄
材盛舉政務尤莫先焉臣等
詎容因循夙弊不能少致裨
益於維新之治於是胥飭胥
勵誓公誓慎命題惟明白正
大不困以所難知校閱雖本
之初試而去留實以中末二
===
試決焉蓋懲夫初學之能道
性命而積學富負挾達世故
者至是始可見也文必根理
必渾厚典則必雄深俊逸必
敷腴鬯達反是而膚淺而詭
誕而衰腐而齪齪者一切弗
取以為一時豪傑庶繇是而

試決焉蓋懲夫初學之能道
性命而積學富負挾達世故
者至是始可見也文必根理
必渾厚典則必雄深俊逸必
敷腴豈達反是而膚淺而詭
誕而衰腐而聱齖者一切弗
取以為一時豪傑庶幾是而
punctuated: 文武大務，恢張一新。況茲掄材盛舉，政務尤莫先焉。臣等詎容因循夙弊，不能少致裨益於維新之治？於是胥飭胥勵，誓公誓慎。命題惟明白正大，不困以所難知。校閱雖本之初試，而去留實以中末二試決焉。蓋懲夫初學之能道性命，而積學富負挾、達世故者，至是始可見也。文必根理，必渾厚典則，必雄深俊逸，必敷腴鬯達。反是而膚淺、而詭誕、而衰腐、而齪齪者，一切弗取。以為一時豪傑，庶繇是而
translation_en: …the great affairs of civil and military government have been expanded and renewed in every respect. How much more, then, does this grand undertaking of selecting talent take precedence among the affairs of government! How could we, your servants, be content to perpetuate longstanding abuses and fail to contribute even a little to this renewed governance? We therefore admonished and encouraged one another, pledging impartiality and care. In setting questions, we sought only clarity, rectitude, and breadth, without placing candidates in difficulty over matters hard to know. Although assessment took the first session as its basis, retention or rejection was in fact decided by the middle and final sessions. This was intended to correct the tendency whereby even beginners could discourse on human nature and destiny, whereas only at this stage could those with accumulated learning, substantial attainments, and an understanding of worldly affairs be discerned. Essays had to be grounded in principle; they had to be substantial, well-rounded, and consonant with classical standards; powerful, profound, distinguished, and untrammeled; ample, rich, fluent, and lucid. Anything contrary to these qualities—superficial, outlandish, stale, or petty—was rejected without exception. We believed that the outstanding talents of the age might thereby…

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
進我
祖宗振古人物之期庶繇是副焉
而我
皇上今兹維新之化庶繇是有以
賛襄光昭之者無窮臣等以
人報
國而尸素之譴庶亦繇是乎可
===
以少逭錄類有序事竣進
御以傳諸天下臣謹述校取之意
用省夫今之與選及夫嗣是
以登者
嘉議大夫掌詹事府事太常
寺卿兼翰林院學士張元禎
謹序

進我
祖宗振古人物之期庶繇是副焉
而我
皇上今茲維新之化庶繇是有以
賛襄光昭之者無窮臣等以
人報
國而𠩄薦之謹庶亦繇是乎可
===
以少逭録類有序事竣進
御以傳諸天下臣謹述校取之意
用省夫今之與選及夫嗣是

嘉議大夫掌詹事府事太常

謹序
punctuated:
進。我祖宗振古人物之期，庶繇是副焉；而我皇上今兹維新之化，庶繇是有以賛襄光昭之者無窮。臣等以人報國，而尸素之譴，庶亦繇是乎可以少逭。錄類有序，事竣進御，以傳諸天下。臣謹述校取之意，用省夫今之與選及夫嗣是以登者。
嘉議大夫、掌詹事府事、太常寺卿兼翰林院學士張元禎謹序。
translation_en:
…advance. May this fulfill our imperial ancestors’ hope for men of a caliber to match antiquity; and may it provide an inexhaustible succession of men to assist and illuminate the renewing influence of our present Emperor. By repaying the state with worthy men, we, your servants, may thereby escape some measure of the reproach of drawing stipends without rendering service. Such records customarily have a preface. Once the work is completed, the record is submitted for imperial inspection and circulated throughout the realm. Your servant has respectfully set forth the intent governing our evaluation and selection, to admonish both those selected now and those who will attain success hereafter.
Preface respectfully composed by Zhang Yuanzhen, Grand Master for Excellent Counsel, in charge of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy.

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Eighteenth Year of Hongzhi (1505)

Officials in Charge of the Examination

Zhang Sheng, Grand Master for Aid in Governance and Minister of Rites, had the courtesy name Qizhao and was from Nancheng County, Jiangxi. He was a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the jichou year.

Li Jie, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Rites, had the courtesy name Shixian and was from Changshu County in the directly administered metropolitan region (Zhili). He was a metropolitan graduate of the bingxu year.

Examiners

Zhang Yuanzhen, Grand Master for Excellent Counsel, Administrator of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Tingxiang and was from Nanchang County, Jiangxi. He was a metropolitan graduate of the gengchen year.

Yang Tinghe, Grand Master for Consultative Service, Grand Secretary of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent [?], and concurrently Hanlin Academician Reader-in-Waiting, had the courtesy name Jiefu and was from Xindu County, Sichuan. He was a metropolitan graduate of the wuxu year.

Associate Examiners

punctuated:
第壹塲

四書

博學而篤志，切問而近思，仁在其中矣。

仁者，人也，親親為大；義者，宜也，尊賢為大。

故將大有為之君，必有所不召之臣；欲有謀焉，則就之。其尊德樂道不如是，不足與有為也。故湯之於伊尹，學焉而後臣之，故不勞而王。

易

天道下濟而光明，地道卑而上行。

先王以茂對時，育萬物。

知周乎萬物，而道濟天下，故不過。

是以立天之道曰陰與陽，立地之道曰柔與剛，立人之道曰仁與義。

書

寬而栗，柔而立，愿而恭，亂而敬，擾而毅，直而溫，簡而廉，剛而塞，彊而義。

古我前后，罔不惟民之承保；后胥慼，鮮以
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Learn broadly and hold firmly to your purpose; inquire earnestly and reflect on what is close at hand. Benevolence lies within these practices.

Benevolence is what makes us human, and loving one’s kin is its greatest expression. Righteousness is doing what is fitting, and honoring the worthy is its greatest expression.

Thus, a ruler who intends to accomplish great things must have ministers whom he does not summon. When he wishes to consult them, he goes to them. Unless he honors virtue and delights in the Way to this degree, he cannot be a partner in great undertakings. Thus Tang learned from Yi Yin before making him his minister, and so attained kingship without toil.

Book of Changes

The Way of Heaven descends to bestow its benefits and shines brightly; the Way of Earth is lowly yet moves upward.

The former kings accordingly responded fully to the seasons and nurtured all things.

His knowledge encompasses all things, and his Way brings benefit to all under Heaven; thus he does not err.

Therefore, they established the Way of Heaven as yin and yang, the Way of Earth as yielding and firm, and the Way of humanity as benevolence and righteousness.

Book of Documents

Be generous yet dignified, gentle yet firm, sincere yet respectful, capable in government yet reverent, tractable yet resolute, upright yet warm, straightforward yet discerning, strong yet substantial, and forceful yet righteous.

In ancient times, our former rulers without exception upheld and protected the people. The rulers all shared this anxious concern, and seldom …

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
不浮于天時
自成湯咸至于帝乙成王畏相惟御事厥
棐有恭不敢自暇自逸矧曰其敢崇
飲越在外服侯甸男衛邦伯越在內
服百僚庶尹惟亞惟服宗工越百姓
里居罔敢湎于酒不惟不敢亦不暇
惟助成王德顯越尹人祇辟
至治馨香感于神明

===
羔羊之皮素絲五紽退食自公委蛇委蛇
雖無予之路車乘馬又何予之玄袞及黼
豈弟君子四方為綱
敬之敬之天維顯思命不易哉無曰高高
在上陟降厥士日監在茲

punctuated:
不浮于天時。

自成湯咸至于帝乙，成王畏相，惟御事厥棐有恭，不敢自暇自逸，矧曰其敢崇飲！越在外服，侯、甸、男、衛、邦伯；越在內服，百僚、庶尹、惟亞、惟服、宗工，越百姓里居，罔敢湎于酒。不惟不敢，亦不暇，惟助成王德顯，越尹人祇辟。

至治馨香，感于神明。

詩

羔羊之皮，素絲五紽。退食自公，委蛇委蛇。

雖無予之，路車乘馬；又何予之？玄袞及黼。

豈弟君子，四方為綱。

敬之敬之！天維顯思，命不易哉！無曰高高在上，陟降厥士，日監在茲。

春秋

公觀魚于棠〔隱公五年〕。

師次于郎，以俟陳人、蔡人〔莊公八年〕。

城費〔襄公七年〕。季孫斯、仲孫何忌帥師墮費。
translation_en:
…not exceed the time allotted by Heaven.

From Cheng Tang down to Di Yi, the accomplished kings held their ministers in awe, while those managing affairs assisted them with reverence. They dared not indulge in leisure or ease; how much less would they dare devote themselves to drinking! In the outer service were the lords of the hou, dian, nan, and wei domains and the regional chiefs; in the inner service were the many officials, the various administrative heads, their deputies, those charged with duties, and the chief officers, together with the many clans dwelling in their communities. None dared abandon themselves to wine. Not only did they dare not: they had no leisure for it. They helped the accomplished kings make their virtue manifest, and those governing the people reverently served their sovereign.

The fragrance of perfect government reaches the spirits and divine powers.

Book of Odes

Lambskin, with five clusters of white silk stitching. Returning from the duke’s court to dine, at ease and composed.

If there is nothing to give him, give him a state carriage and a team of four horses. What else shall be given him? A dark dragon robe and an axe-patterned garment.

The gracious and affable gentleman serves as the guiding cord for the four quarters.

Be reverent, be reverent! Heaven is indeed manifest; its mandate is not easy to retain! Do not say that it is high, high above: it ascends and descends, attending to affairs [?], daily watching here.

Spring and Autumn Annals

The duke watched the fishing at Tang. 〔Fifth year of Duke Yin.〕

The army encamped at Lang to await the men of Chen and Cai. 〔Eighth year of Duke Zhuang.〕

Bi was fortified. 〔Seventh year of Duke Xiang.〕 Jisun Si and Zhongsun Heji led troops to demolish the fortifications of Bi.…

translation_en:
…without going through the doorway.

Movement and stillness occur between Heaven and Earth.

Heaven shelters without partiality; Earth supports without partiality; the sun and moon shine without partiality. Upholding these three principles to serve all under Heaven is called the three forms of impartiality.

That which brings forth the myriad things is sageliness.

Second Session

Discourse

Centrality is the great foundation of all under Heaven.

Imperial Edicts, Proclamations, and Memorials 〔One topic from one category〕

Compose an edict in the voice of the Han emperor ordering the commanderies and kingdoms to seek worthy men who have been overlooked. 〔Eleventh year of Emperor Gao〕

Compose a proclamation in the voice of the Tang emperor appointing Zhang Jiuling as Director of the Secretariat. 〔Twenty-second year of Kaiyuan〕

Compose a memorial in the voice of Fan Zhen, Administrator of the Bureau of Policy Criticism under the Song, requesting the establishment within the palace of a register of memorials submitted to the throne. 〔Second year of Zhihe〕

Legal Judgments 〔Five items〕

Recommending and employing officials and clerks with past offenses.

Inequitable assignment of laborers to service.

Prohibiting the heterodox arts of ritual masters and spirit mediums.

Allowing soldiers to absent themselves from duty.

text:
織造違禁叚疋
第叄塲
策〔五道〕
問用人理財二者治天下之先務也我
太祖立國之初建官府制財用一以周官之法
為準官有定員賦有定額觀於諸司職
掌所載槩可見矣當時人才之用各稱
其職而賢鄙不至於同滯軍國之需隨
取各足而公私不至於困乏至於今日
===
乃有或變其初者自朝著以至州縣之
間員外之官幾倍於舊是亦足以待天
下之才矣而一歲之選不足以盡一歲
之人一登選籍輙有淹滯之嘆自山澤
關市之課州縣帑藏之積盡取以歸於
京師是亦足以周天下之用矣而一歲
之入不足以供一歲之費每一舉事輙
有困乏之虞夫人才則病其或多財用
則病其或少多者思以損之少者思以

問：用人理財二者，治天下之先務也。我太祖立國之初，建官府，制財用，一以周官之法為準。官有定員，賦有定額，觀於諸司職掌所載，槩可見矣。當時人才之用，各稱其職，而賢鄙不至於同滯；軍國之需，隨取各足，而公私不至於困乏。至於今日，乃有或變其初者。自朝著以至州縣之間，員外之官幾倍於舊，是亦足以待天下之才矣，而一歲之選不足以盡一歲之人，一登選籍，輙有淹滯之嘆。自山澤關市之課、州縣帑藏之積，盡取以歸於京師，是亦足以周天下之用矣，而一歲之入不足以供一歲之費，每一舉事，輙有困乏之虞。夫人才則病其或多，財用則病其或少。多者思以損之，少者思以

Weaving bolts of silk in violation of prohibitions.

Third Session
Policy Questions 〔Five questions〕

Question: Employing men and managing finances are the two foremost tasks in governing the realm. When our Emperor Taizu founded the dynasty, he established government offices and regulated expenditure, taking the institutions of the Offices of Zhou as his standard throughout. Offices had fixed staffing levels, and taxes had fixed quotas. This can be seen in broad outline from what is recorded in the Duties of the Various Offices (Zhusi zhizhang). At that time, talented men were employed in positions suited to their abilities, and the worthy and the unworthy did not alike languish awaiting appointment. The needs of the military and the state were adequately met whenever resources were drawn upon, and neither public nor private resources were reduced to penury.

Today, however, some things have departed from those original arrangements. From the imperial court down to the prefectures and counties, officials beyond the established complement number several times as many as before. This should suffice to accommodate the realm’s talented men. Yet the appointments made in a year cannot absorb all the men available that year; once a man enters the appointment registers, he immediately has cause to lament prolonged delay. Revenues from mountains and marshes, customs barriers and markets, together with the funds accumulated in prefectural and county treasuries, are all taken and remitted to the capital. This should suffice to meet the realm’s expenses. Yet a year’s revenue cannot cover a year’s expenditure; whenever an undertaking is initiated, there is immediately fear of a shortage.

As for talented men, the concern is that there may be too many; as for financial resources, the concern is that there may be too few. For what is excessive, one considers reducing it; for what is insufficient, one considers how to …

text:
益之二者之說不知其可不可也如之
何而可以復職掌之舊執事者願有聞
也
問自古人君之致盛治未有不本於君臣
之相與者虞廷載賡之歌周人燕樂之
雅至今誦之猶可想見其當時之盛嗣
是而後上下之交不同而事功之成亦
異或以受奏而止輦或因直諫而罷朝
或詰責於四事之啓陳或嘉納於十事
===
之要說稱名之誤便至叱廢而亦有奏
事不應特蒙優任者延英之對流汗霑
衣而亦有侍從陳言温顏訪問者若是
者是或一道也恭惟我
太祖高皇帝屈羣策以定天下一時
君臣同遊之盛雖今日不能盡知而
五倫一書所載猶可窺見其一二人誦家傳
萬代如見此
盛德大業之所由成也今

益之。二者之說，不知其可不可也。如之何而可以復職掌之舊？執事者願有聞也。

問：自古人君之致盛治，未有不本於君臣之相與者。虞廷載賡之歌，周人燕樂之雅，至今誦之，猶可想見其當時之盛。嗣是而後，上下之交不同，而事功之成亦異。或以受奏而止輦，或因直諫而罷朝，或詰責於四事之啓陳，或嘉納於十事之要說。稱名之誤，便至叱廢，而亦有奏事不應，特蒙優任者；延英之對，流汗霑衣，而亦有侍從陳言，温顏訪問者。若是者，是或一道也。恭惟我太祖高皇帝，屈羣策以定天下。一時君臣同遊之盛，雖今日不能盡知，而《五倫》一書所載，猶可窺見其一二。人誦家傳，萬代如見，此盛德大業之所由成也。今
translation_en:
…increase it. Whether these two proposals are practicable, we do not know. How might the former arrangements for official responsibilities be restored? Those charged with this matter would welcome instruction.

Question: Since antiquity, no ruler has brought about flourishing government without grounding it in the relationship between sovereign and ministers. The songs sung and continued in response at the court of Shun, and the Zhou court hymns for banqueting and merriment, still allow us, when reciting them today, to imagine the flourishing conditions of their time. Thereafter, relations between superiors and subordinates differed, and so too did their achievements. One ruler halted his imperial carriage to receive a memorial; another dismissed court because of forthright remonstrance. One reproached a minister for presenting four matters; another approvingly accepted a concise exposition of ten matters. An error in addressing someone by name could bring a rebuke and dismissal; yet there were also those who failed to answer while reporting affairs and nevertheless received exceptional favor and continued employment. Some, when answering questions in Yanying Hall, sweated until their robes were soaked; yet there were also attendant officials who offered their views and were questioned with a kindly expression. Such instances perhaps represent a single way [?]. Reverently we reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao drew upon the counsels of many to bring peace to the realm. Although we cannot now fully know the splendor of the fellowship between ruler and ministers in that time, the records in the book The Five Relationships (Wulun) still offer glimpses of it. Recited by individuals and transmitted in households, they make those events seem present to ten thousand generations. This was how such abundant virtue and great accomplishments came to fruition. title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
明天子在上恪遵
聖謨勵精圖治退
朝之暇數延羣臣咨訪治理天下聞之皆欣
欣然相慶以為不世之遇芹曝之私竊
思所以將順
德美之萬一者展轉於中而未之有得也諸士
子觀光而來目擊其盛必有先得我心
之所同然者矣請稽之往迹參之時宜
試以告我明當入對
大廷執此以往可也
問人主之學舍經史無所用其心者羅仲
素謂讀經以尚書為先讀史以唐書為
首夫六經皆二帝三王致治之法萬世不可
易者諸史則歷代興亡之迹存焉其有
資於治一也而仲素之言獨先於二書
者何居蔡沈序書傳以帝王之治本於
此心之存亡范祖禹序唐鑑以一代之
得失歸於君子小人之用舍其論治亂

問：人主之學，舍經史無所用其心者。羅仲素謂讀經以《尚書》為先，讀史以《唐書》為首。夫六經皆二帝三王致治之法，萬世不可易者；諸史則歷代興亡之迹存焉。其有資於治一也，而仲素之言獨先於二書者，何居？蔡沈序《書傳》，以帝王之治本於此心之存亡；范祖禹序《唐鑑》，以一代之得失歸於君子小人之用舍。其論治亂
translation_en:
…the enlightened Son of Heaven reigns above, reverently following the sage counsels and devoting himself earnestly to good government. In his leisure after court, he frequently summons his ministers to consult them about governance. All under Heaven, hearing this, rejoice and congratulate one another, regarding it as an opportunity rarely encountered in an age. With the humble wish to offer celery or the warmth of the sun, I have privately pondered how I might support even one ten-thousandth part of his excellent virtue. These thoughts turn over within me, but I have yet to arrive at an answer. You candidates have come to behold the splendor of the realm and have witnessed its flourishing firsthand. Surely some of you have already grasped what our minds would alike approve. Please examine the precedents of the past, weigh them against the needs of the present, and set forth your views for me. When you enter the great court to respond to the sovereign, you may take these ideas with you.

Question: In a ruler’s learning, apart from the classics and histories, there is nothing to which he should devote his mind. Luo Zhongsu said that, in reading the classics, one should begin with the Book of Documents (Shangshu), and, in reading history, with the History of the Tang (Tangshu). Now, the Six Classics all contain the methods by which the Two Emperors and Three Kings achieved good government, methods unalterable for ten thousand generations; the histories preserve the record of the rise and fall of successive dynasties. They are alike in contributing to governance. Why, then, did Zhongsu give priority specifically to these two books? In his preface to the Commentary on the Book of Documents (Shu zhuan), Cai Shen held that imperial and royal government rests upon whether this moral mind is preserved or lost. In his preface to the Mirror of the Tang (Tang jian), Fan Zuyu attributed the successes and failures of a dynasty to the employment or dismissal of exemplary and petty men. In their discussions of order and disorder…

小人之用舎其關𠘧於人主之心何如
也諸士子試以二書所載摘其存亡用
舎之大者比而論之將獻之以為
聖學之助
問昔人有云大小之事皆須用智又云成
大事者在膽凡事之來有智可料有膽
可决其意固善矣然智稱有餘者足以
相國號為智囊者又足以亡身智果足
===

者又足以亡國膽果可恃哉用智用膽

言事皆用智矣其身之自用何事可徴
能言成事在膽矣其身之自成何事最
著其所謂智所謂膽亦各因其性之所
長而言之歟抑於聖賢之學有所得而
為是說也茲欲所用皆善而無其弊何
為而可願明言之亦他日受大任重之

問：昔人有云：「大小之事皆須用智。」又云：「成大事者在膽。」凡事之來，有智可料，有膽可决，其意固善矣。然智稱有餘者足以相國，號為智囊者又足以亡身，智果足尚哉？一身是膽者足以卻敵，膽大如斗者又足以亡國，膽果可恃哉？用智用膽之善，成功何如？其不善也，流弊安極？能言事皆用智矣，其身之自用，何事可徴？能言成事在膽矣，其身之自成，何事最著？其所謂智、所謂膽，亦各因其性之所長而言之歟？抑於聖賢之學有所得而為是說也？茲欲所用皆善而無其弊，何為而可？願明言之，亦他日受大任重之
translation_en:
…in matters of success and failure, their views again seem to differ. Yet what bearing does the employment or dismissal of gentlemen and petty men have upon the ruler’s mind [?]? You candidates should select from the records of these two books the most significant instances concerning the preservation or loss of the mind and the employment or dismissal of men, and compare and discuss them. Your answers will be presented to assist His Majesty’s learning.
Question: Someone of old said, “In affairs great and small, one must always use wisdom.” Another said, “Accomplishing great affairs depends on courage.” When any affair arises, wisdom enables one to assess it, and courage enables one to decide. The intent of these sayings is certainly good. Yet one praised as having wisdom to spare was able to serve as chief minister, while another, called a “bag of wisdom,” brought about his own destruction. Is wisdom indeed worthy of esteem? One described as “courage through and through” was able to repel the enemy, while another, whose “courage was as great as a peck measure,” brought his state to ruin. Can courage indeed be relied upon? When wisdom and courage are used well, what successes do they achieve? When used badly, where do their harmful consequences end? The man who could say that all affairs require wisdom—what deeds attest to his own use of it? The man who could say that accomplishment depends on courage—what were his own most notable achievements? Did each speak of what he called wisdom or courage according to the particular strengths of his disposition? Or did they formulate these sayings because they had gained some understanding of the learning of the sages and worthies? If we now wish to ensure that both are always used well, without their attendant harms, how can this be accomplished? Explain this clearly; it will also bear upon your future service in positions of great responsibility and weighty…

問：邊備之務有四，曰選將也、治兵也、屯田也、馬政也。是四者，其事體雖異，而皆於禦備爲要，不可以緩急先後言。如人之一身，耳目手足之用不同，舉其一，則以類而應，有不可相無者。惟我先朝畫一之法具在，馴至今日，補偏救弊之政，日講月求，蓋詳以盡。如重武舉之選、下招募之令、命使之驗屯、出憲臣之專馬政，皆近日事也。其後效必有可觀者，而議者尚復云云，豈事者不能自信也？諸生學通達國體者，於此必計之熟矣。幸證言之，將以轉聞于上。

…a foundation for this.

Question: There are four tasks in frontier defense: selecting commanders, training troops, maintaining military agricultural colonies, and administering horse supplies. Although these four differ in their particulars, all are essential to defense; they cannot be ranked by urgency or priority. They are like the ears, eyes, hands, and feet of a single body: their functions differ, but when one is brought into action, the others respond in accordance with their kind, and none can dispense with the others. The uniform regulations established by our former imperial reigns remain fully in place. Over time, down to the present, measures to redress imbalances and remedy abuses have been discussed daily and sought monthly, with thoroughness and comprehensiveness. Giving greater weight to selection through the military examinations, issuing orders for recruitment, commissioning envoys to inspect military agricultural colonies, and dispatching censorial officials to take exclusive charge of horse administration are all recent initiatives. Their subsequent results should surely be worthy of attention. Yet critics continue to raise objections. Could it be that those conducting these affairs cannot themselves be confident? Those among you candidates whose learning encompasses the workings of the state must have considered these matters carefully. Please set forth your views with supporting evidence, so that they may be conveyed to His Majesty.

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
博學而篤志切問而近思仁在其中矣
謝遷
同考試官主事劉批平平寫出而趣味
洒落自爾完好此士必才性功力兩到者
同考試官編修李批仁在其中正為學
有得處子能言之豈亦有得者耶
同考試官編修賈批說理文字精到似
無可以減矣
===
同考試官左中允傅批題本平易人人知
之理明盡言詞発潔如此作者亦不多見
考試官學士楊批語意完潔
考試官學士張批能說出子夏語意
人能從事於學則仁不外是矣蓋學本以致知
非為仁也然能從事於此則心有所存仁豈不
由是而可得哉子夏勉人之為學切矣吾想其
意蓋謂求仁之功雖不止於講學而講學之事

punctuated:
第壹場

四書

博學而篤志，切問而近思，仁在其中矣。

謝遷

同考試官主事劉批：「平平寫出，而趣味洒落，自爾完好。此士必才性功力兩到者。」

同考試官編修李批：「仁在其中，正為學有得處。子能言之，豈亦有得者耶？」

同考試官編修賈批：「說理文字精到，似無可以減矣。」

同考試官左中允傅批：「題本平易，人人知之。理明盡，言詞発潔如此，作者亦不多見。」

考試官學士楊批：「語意完潔。」

考試官學士張批：「能說出子夏語意。」

人能從事於學，則仁不外是矣。蓋學本以致知，非為仁也。然能從事於此，則心有所存，仁豈不由是而可得哉？子夏勉人之為學切矣！吾想其意，蓋謂求仁之功雖不止於講學，而講學之事
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“Learn broadly and be steadfast in purpose; inquire earnestly and reflect on what is close at hand: benevolence lies therein.”

Xie Qian 謝遷

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Secretary: “Written with simplicity, yet its flavor is free and unencumbered, and it is naturally complete and sound. This scholar must be accomplished both in native talent and in sustained effort.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Compiler: “‘Benevolence lies therein’ points precisely to where learning yields genuine attainment. Since you can articulate this, might you too have attained it?”

Comment by Associate Examiner Jia, Compiler: “The exposition of principle is so precise and accomplished that there seems to be nothing one could cut.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Fu, Left Mentor: “The topic is straightforward and familiar to everyone. Yet writers who explain its principles so clearly and fully, with wording so lucid and concise [?], are seldom seen.”

Comment by Examiner Yang, Academician: “The wording and meaning are complete and concise.”

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Academician: “He succeeds in expressing the meaning of Zixia’s words.”

If a person can devote himself to learning, benevolence lies within this very activity. Learning is fundamentally directed toward extending knowledge, rather than practicing benevolence. Yet if one can devote oneself to it, the mind has something to hold fast to; how could benevolence not be attained through this? How earnestly Zixia urges people to learn! As I conceive his meaning, he is saying that although the work of seeking benevolence is not confined to the study and discussion of learning, the activity of such study and discussion…

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
實有資於為仁何則理散於天下而萃於吾心
人不可不學也而患其不博學博則詩書六藝
無不考前言徃行無不識而有融會貫通之地
焉學不可無志也而患其不篤志篤則專一以
必期其至懇切以必要其成而無苟且作輟之
弊焉以至學有所疑也非問莫釋然不可失之
泛濫或質於師或辯於友務求着己而弗切弗
問也學有未得也非思莫致然不可索之高遠
或溫其故或繹其新務求近裏而弗近弗思也
===
夫學焉而博志焉而篤則心惟在是而不他適
問焉而切思焉而近則心惟在是而不外馳是
雖未及乎力行而為仁然仁人心也心既不他
適則操存自熟天理由之而日明仁不即寓於
博學篤志中乎是雖未至於實踐而為仁然仁
心德也心既不外馳則涵養自熟人欲由之而
日消仁不即存於切問近思中乎是則因講學
之事得為仁之功仁豈遠於我而學豈無益於
仁哉子夏勉人之意如此抑即是論之聖門之

必期其至懇切以必要其成而無苟且作輟之
弊焉以至學有所疑也非問莫釋然不可失之
泛濫或質於師或辯於友務求着己而弗切弗
問也學有未得也非思莫致然不可索之高遠
或遍其故或繹其新務求通裏而弗近弗思也
===
夫學焉而博志焉而篤則心惟在是而不他適
問焉而切思焉而近則心惟在是而不外馳是
雖未及乎力行而爲仁然仁人心也心既不他
適則操存自熟天理由之而日明仁不即寓於
博學篤志中乎是雖未至於實踐而爲仁然仁
心德也心既不外馳則涵養自熟人欲由之而
日消仁不即存於切問近思中乎是則因講學
之事得爲仁之功仁豈遠於我而學豈無益於
仁哉子夏勉人之意如此抑即是論之聖門之
punctuated:
實有資於為仁。何則？理散於天下，而萃於吾心，人不可不學也，而患其不博。學博，則詩書六藝無不考，前言徃行無不識，而有融會貫通之地焉。學不可無志也，而患其不篤。志篤，則專一以必期其至，懇切以必要其成，而無苟且作輟之弊焉。以至學有所疑也，非問莫釋，然不可失之泛濫；或質於師，或辯於友，務求着己，而弗切弗問也。學有未得也，非思莫致，然不可索之高遠；或溫其故，或繹其新，務求近裏，而弗近弗思也。
夫學焉而博，志焉而篤，則心惟在是而不他適；問焉而切，思焉而近，則心惟在是而不外馳。是雖未及乎力行而為仁，然仁，人心也。心既不他適，則操存自熟，天理由之而日明，仁不即寓於博學篤志中乎？是雖未至於實踐而為仁，然仁，心德也。心既不外馳，則涵養自熟，人欲由之而日消，仁不即存於切問近思中乎？是則因講學之事，得為仁之功，仁豈遠於我，而學豈無益於仁哉？子夏勉人之意如此。抑即是論之，聖門之
translation_en:
…does indeed contribute to the practice of benevolence. Why is this? Principle is dispersed throughout the world yet gathered within our own minds. One cannot dispense with learning; the concern is that it may lack breadth. When learning is broad, one examines everything in the Odes, the Documents, and the Six Arts, and knows the words and deeds of earlier people, thereby gaining a foundation for integrating them into a coherent understanding. Learning cannot be without resolve; the concern is that this resolve may lack firmness. When resolve is firm, one concentrates single-mindedly, determined to reach the goal, and applies oneself earnestly, determined to achieve success, without the faults of careless effort or intermittent application. Furthermore, when doubts arise in learning, only questioning can resolve them; yet one must not err by ranging indiscriminately. Whether consulting a teacher or debating with friends, one must seek what bears upon oneself, asking nothing that is not pertinent. When something in learning remains uncomprehended, only reflection can bring understanding; yet one must not seek it in what is lofty and remote. Whether reviewing what one already knows or drawing out the implications of something new, one must seek what touches one's inner self, reflecting on nothing that is not close at hand.
When learning is broad and resolve firm, the mind remains wholly engaged in these things and turns nowhere else. When questions are pertinent and reflection concerns what is close at hand, the mind remains wholly engaged in these things and does not race outward. Although this has not yet reached the stage of vigorously acting to practice benevolence, benevolence is the human mind. Once the mind no longer turns elsewhere, holding fast to and preserving it naturally becomes a mastered practice, and heavenly principle thereby grows clearer each day. Does benevolence not reside precisely within broad learning and firm resolve? Although this has not yet reached the stage of practicing benevolence through actual conduct, benevolence is the virtue of the mind. Once the mind no longer races outward, nurturing it naturally becomes a mastered practice, and human desires thereby diminish each day. Does benevolence not reside precisely within pertinent questioning and reflection on what is close at hand? Thus, through the work of studying and discussing learning, one gains the efficacy of cultivating benevolence. How could benevolence be far from us, and how could learning fail to benefit benevolence? Such was Zixia's intention in encouraging others. Yet, considering the matter on this basis, the learning of the sage's school…

translation_en:
…learning consists solely in the mind. Pursuing learning and practicing benevolence are not two separate undertakings. Pursuing learning aims to comprehend fully within this mind all principles; practicing benevolence aims to leave not a single impurity in this mind. Learning is the initial endeavor toward benevolence; benevolence is the ultimate achievement of learning. One must pursue learning to clarify these principles in the mind, then earnestly practice them to seek their fullest realization. Zixia’s statement that “benevolence lies within these” might seem to distinguish an inner from an outer realm. Master Cheng said that this is the Way that penetrates the highest and the lowest alike. Students should ponder it deeply.
“Benevolence means being human; loving one’s kin is its greatest expression. Righteousness means what is fitting; honoring the worthy is its greatest expression.”
Lin Wendi

Comment by Associate Examiner Sun, Hanlin Compiler: Plain and accessible yet classically elegant language; substantial and profound learning. Here is someone who speaks well of benevolence and righteousness.
Comment by Associate Examiner Mao, Hanlin Reader-in-waiting: Few explain ‘human’ and ‘fitting’ with precision and pertinence. This composition uses words economically, yet the underlying coherence of the Way is evident of itself. Its conclusion also reaches a definite resolution. Has its author perhaps devoted himself to investigating the Learning of Principle?

text:
大者甚矣仁義之切於身與事也然其所施則
孰有大於親親尊賢者哉孔子答哀公問政之
意如此蓋嘗論之人君之為政也修身必本於
道修道必本於仁仁之為言人之身也在天為
生物之心在人即有生之理理寓於人自然有
惻怛之意而形與理不相離也人具此理油然
有慈愛之情而理與形無或間也仁之切於身
者如此自其所施而言之則或為萬民之仁或

而天倫之恩重由是推之以仁民而民無不仁

於親親者乎然五性之中仁必有義義之為言

自其所施而言之則或為萬民之正或為萬物

translation_en: …great applications. How intimately benevolence and righteousness concern the person and affairs! Yet among their applications, what could be greater than loving one’s kin and honoring the worthy? Such was the meaning of Confucius’s reply when Duke Ai asked about government. Let us consider this: when a ruler governs, cultivating his person must be rooted in the Way, and cultivating the Way must be rooted in benevolence. Benevolence refers to the human person. In Heaven it is the heart that gives life to things; in human beings it is the principle of life. When this principle resides in a person, feelings of compassion arise naturally, and bodily form and principle are inseparable. Possessing this principle, a person spontaneously feels affection and love, and principle and bodily form are never divided. Such is the intimate relation of benevolence to the person. In its application, it may take the form of benevolence toward all the people or love for all things: these are all functions of benevolence. Its greatest application, however, has a particular locus. One must be devoted to one’s single ancestral root, so that the authenticity of one’s Heaven-given nature is preserved in full, and maintain harmony among the nine degrees of kinship, so that the affection inherent in familial relationships is deepened. From this foundation, one extends benevolence to the people, leaving none without its care, and extends love to things, leaving none unloved. Among the applications of benevolence, what could be greater than loving one’s kin? Yet among the five moral qualities of human nature, benevolence necessarily entails righteousness. Righteousness means what is appropriate in affairs. In affairs there is a determinate principle; in human beings there are responses to myriad changes. One analyzes what is right and what is wrong, distinguishing them sharply so that neither can be interchanged; one judges what is acceptable and what is not, distinguishing them clearly so that each judgment is fitting. Such is the intimate relation of righteousness to affairs. In its application, it may take the form of rectifying all the people or benefiting all things: these are all functions of righteousness. 必精於鑒別而惟有道者之是崇隆其體貌而
惟有德者之是貴由是藉之以正民而民無不
正也藉之以利物而物無不利也義之施孰有
大於尊賢者乎是則知親親為仁之大則由仁
以脩身者必自親親始知尊賢為義之大則由
義以親親者必自尊賢始哀公果能從事於此
則有君有臣而政豈有不舉者哉抑嘗通考此
章之言而知孔子之政矣舉天下國家之大而
歸之九經舉九經之要而本之脩身舉脩身之
===
道而歸之達道達德而又本之禮義二者而發
端於仁之一言焉可謂至博而至約者矣哀公
親問於孔子而不能用此魯之所以不競也歟
故將大有為之君必有所不召之臣欲有
謀焉則就之其尊德樂道不如是不足與
有為也故湯之於伊尹學焉而後臣之故
不勞而王

同考試官郎中周　　　　　　　　　安譽
punctuated:
必精於鑒別，而惟有道者之是崇；隆其體貌，而惟有德者之是貴。由是藉之以正民，而民無不正也；藉之以利物，而物無不利也。義之施，孰有大於尊賢者乎？是則知親親為仁之大，則由仁以脩身者必自親親始；知尊賢為義之大，則由義以親親者必自尊賢始。哀公果能從事於此，則有君有臣，而政豈有不舉者哉？抑嘗通考此章之言，而知孔子之政矣。舉天下國家之大，而歸之九經；舉九經之要，而本之脩身；舉脩身之道，而歸之達道、達德，而又本之禮義二者，而發端於仁之一言焉。可謂至博而至約者矣！哀公親問於孔子而不能用，此魯之所以不競也歟？
故將大有為之君，必有所不召之臣；欲有謀焉，則就之。其尊德樂道不如是，不足與有為也。故湯之於伊尹，學焉而後臣之，故不勞而王。
安磐
同考試官郎中周
translation_en:
…one must exercise discerning judgment, honoring only those who possess the Way, and accord them elevated ceremonial treatment, esteeming only those who possess virtue. By relying on them to rectify the people, none among the people will fail to be rectified; by relying on them to benefit all things, nothing will fail to receive benefit. What exercise of righteousness could be greater than honoring the worthy? Thus, knowing that affection for one’s kin is the greatest expression of benevolence, those who cultivate themselves through benevolence must begin with affection for their kin. Knowing that honoring the worthy is the greatest expression of righteousness, those who show affection for their kin through righteousness must begin with honoring the worthy. If Duke Ai could truly devote himself to this, ruler and ministers would each fulfill their roles: how could government fail to be carried out? Moreover, having examined the words of this chapter as a whole, I have come to understand Confucius’s approach to government. The vast affairs of the world, the state, and the family are brought together in the nine guiding principles; the essentials of these nine principles are rooted in self-cultivation. The way of self-cultivation is brought together in the universally applicable ways and virtues, and further rooted in the two things, ritual propriety and righteousness, while its starting point is the single word ‘benevolence.’ This may indeed be called supremely comprehensive yet supremely concise! Duke Ai personally questioned Confucius but could not put his teaching into practice. Was this not why Lu failed to grow strong?
“Thus a ruler who intends to accomplish great things must have ministers whom he does not summon. If he wishes to consult them, he goes to them. Unless he honors virtue and delights in the Way to this degree, he cannot be helped to accomplish great things. Thus Tang first studied under Yi Yin and only afterward made him his minister; hence he attained kingship without toil.”
An Pan.

…few who accommodate [?]. This composition’s language and meaning unfold with subtlety, vividly evoking the manner in which Jing Chou was instructed at the time. Its author has evidently gained insight through emulating the ancient worthies.
Associate Examiner Bi, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: On topics from the Mencius, writers whose prose is straightforward and vigorous are quite capable of developing an argument; but can one often find a piece whose language and purport are as refined and rigorous as this one?
Examiner Yang, a Hanlin Academician, comments: Plain and fluent.
Examiner Zhang, a Hanlin Academician, comments: An exposition of the meaning should be written precisely like this.
When the great worthy discussed a ruler’s plans for good government, he located their basis in honoring the worthy; when he adduced the former sage’s achievement of good government, he likewise traced its foundation to honoring the worthy. Indeed, in planning good government, nothing takes precedence over honoring the worthy. Does not consideration of Cheng Tang’s honoring of Yi Yin make this all the more convincing? Formerly, when Mencius explained to Jing Chou why the king of Qi should not summon him, he reached this point: obtaining worthy men is the first task of governing, and honoring them is a ruler’s great virtue. Thus a ruler who would accomplish great things, intending to advance the Way, achieve good government, and establish extraordinary merit, must humble himself and set aside his position of power toward worthy ministers with whom he can accomplish such things, showing them the respect of refraining from summoning them. When there is a major affair of government, he goes to them in person to plan its successful completion; though this means a superior showing respect to an inferior, he does not demur. When there is a great uncertainty, he goes to consult them and settle the deliberation; though this means one of exalted rank deferring to one of low rank, he gives it no concern. The reason for this is not that the worthy minister makes himself exalted and important. In his heart he thinks: ‘What binds me to my ruler is virtue. If his honoring of virtue does not …’

如是焉則尚賢之念微矣何足與共濟邪君之
重乎我者以道也其樂道不如是焉則好善之
心替矣奚足與有為邪蓋嘗觀諸成湯之於伊
尹矣成湯大有為之君也伊尹所不召之臣也
三聘之勤待以不臣之禮一德之妙孚於受學
之餘師賓自得即先覺之天民也而尊之也至
厥辟左右即聿求之元聖也而任之也專於是

不自勞而臣有成功之助尊賢之效一至于此

translation_en:
…in this way, then his regard for the worthy is slight. How could he be someone with whom to accomplish great things? What makes the ruler value me is the Way. If his delight in the Way does not reach this degree, then his love of goodness has declined. How could he be someone with whom to undertake great deeds?

Consider Cheng Tang’s treatment of Yi Yin. Cheng Tang was a ruler of great achievements; Yi Yin was a minister whom he would not summon. Through the diligence of three invitations, he treated Yi Yin with a courtesy that did not place him in the position of a subject. The subtle unity of their virtue was realized through Tang’s receiving instruction. At ease as teacher and honored guest, Yi Yin was a man of Heaven who had awakened first to the Way, and Tang honored him to the utmost. Attending his sovereign on either side, he was the great sage whom Tang had sought, and Tang entrusted him with undivided responsibility. Thus, ruler and minister shared one purpose, and good government began in a territory of seventy li. Their Ways accorded, and eleven punitive expeditions met with no opposition. Tang gathered Heaven’s great mandate upon himself, and bringing the realm to settled order required no toil [?]. He succeeded to the dominion formerly held by Xia, and completing his kingly enterprise proved no difficulty.

Thus, at the outset, the minister could not simply be summoned, while the ruler possessed genuine sincerity in honoring the worthy. In the end, the ruler did not have to toil himself, while the minister helped him achieve success. Such were the far-reaching effects of honoring the worthy! Yet the king of Qi wished to use his rank to slight a man of virtue. Why indeed was this?

Still, Mencius spoke these words for a particular purpose. In the relationship between ruler and minister, how could there be a rigid distinction between teacher and subject? On hearing excellent counsel, the ruler bowed twice, without considering this improper toward his minister. In speaking forth and knocking his head to the ground, the minister likewise considered there to be no impropriety toward his ruler. In essence, one takes goodness as one’s teacher without confining oneself to any fixed person. Even treating someone as a minister can therefore be a means of treating him as a teacher. Mencius’s words addressed the circumstances of his time. Those described as preferring to take as ministers the people whom they themselves have taught might surely be moved by them!

This composition is clear in principle and vigorous in expression. Compared with essays assembled from borrowed formulas, it is like pearls beside rubble. Anyone with eyes can recognize its value. Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Hanlin Compiler: Its exposition of the sage’s achievement in nurturing things resembles a gentle spring wind and timely rain: vitality wells forth abundantly, and nothing lies outside the great work of creation.

Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Hanlin Reader-in-Waiting: The vast efficacy of the sage’s utmost sincerity is inherently difficult to comprehend. This essay examines principle with precision, and its prose adequately conveys that understanding. It certainly deserves inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Yang, Hanlin Academician: It captures the purport of Master Zhu’s Original Meaning of the Book of Changes.

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Hanlin Academician: Its reasoning reaches the heart of the matter, and its expression is adequate to it—a rare achievement.

The sage embodies the Image of the hexagram Wuwang, “Without Falsehood,” faithfully carrying out Heaven’s intent and bringing the natures of things to full realization. I act on Heaven’s behalf in ordering things; if even one thing fails to find its proper place, who bears responsibility? Thus they made sincerity their guiding principle and assisted the transforming process, deeply embodying its intent to generate and develop things without contravening it. The great creative power bestows its gifts, and nothing lies outside its nurture. I carry out my work in obedience to Heaven; if even one thing fails to fulfill its life, who bears the blame? Thus, through earnestness and integrity, they moved things to respond, fully meeting the seasons of nurture without departing from them. In this way they participated in Heaven’s work: Heaven gives things life, and I nurture them. Heaven and I may seem far apart in position, yet, like parents and their principal son, our hearts naturally accord as one. Through this unity I bring the myriad things together: they arise together, and I nurture them all. Things and I may seem separate in bodily form, yet, as my siblings and companions, we naturally share the circulation of a single vital energy.

People have their human nature, and the means by which the kings cherished and nurtured them were comprehensive. Once the people were numerous, they enriched them; once prosperous, they educated them. All this simply followed their natural tendencies. How could selfishness be allowed to intervene? Things have their respective natures, and the means by which the kings protected them reached everywhere. They established regulations for each matter and safeguards for every particular, simply following things’ inherent nature. How could contrived intentions intervene?

是以立天之道曰陰與陽，立地之道曰柔與剛，立人之道曰仁與義。
孫紹先

同考試官編修陳批：「締構嚴整，有節有度，而神采朗潤，良邁心於性命之學者。」
同考試官侍讀徐批：「歷叙三才之道，明白簡當，無一長語。非深於易者，能有此作哉？」

…Yet in their hearts they never regarded this as an achievement of their own. Heaven endowed them generously and expected much of them. Because its endowment was generous, the former kings alone could bring to fulfillment the natures that the myriad things could not themselves fulfill. Because its expectations were profound, everything the former kings did to fulfill what the myriad things could not fulfill themselves arose simply from their clear recognition of what their allotted duties required, and of responsibilities they could not decline. Thus the former kings took Heaven’s heart as their own [?]. How could they have acted with a calculated purpose, seeking to claim an achievement before all under Heaven?
“Thus, establishing the Way of Heaven, they called it yin and yang; establishing the Way of Earth, they called it yielding and firm; establishing the Way of humanity, they called it benevolence and righteousness.”
Sun Shaoxian
Comment by Associate Examiner Ren, Chief Supervising Secretary: “His independently acquired learning is [illegible] in his writing. Compared with rustic people judging a jade disk, raising or lowering their appraisal with the crowd, he is decidedly different. His talent and spirit are commendable.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Compiler: “The composition is rigorous and orderly, well articulated and proportioned, while its spirit is luminous and refined. He is indeed one who applies his mind to the study of human nature and destiny [?].”
Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Reader-in-waiting: “He sets forth in turn the Ways of the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—clearly, concisely, and aptly, without a single superfluous phrase. Could anyone without a profound understanding of the Book of Changes produce such a work?”

莊重不凡不凡
論三才之所以立一性命之理也夫天有陰陽
地有剛柔人有仁義此三才之所以立也然何
莫而非性命之理哉且夫性命之理其大原出
於天地其全體具於吾人是故形於上者為天
不徒依乎形而已也其為圜為君之表必有道

論三才之所以立，一性命之理也。夫天有陰陽，地有剛柔，人有仁義，此三才之所以立也。然何莫而非性命之理哉？且夫性命之理，其大原出於天地，其全體具於吾人。是故形於上者為天，不徒依乎形而已也。其為圜為君之表，必有道以妙用乎萬化，是天之所以立也，而陰陽盡之矣。盖靜而為陰，動而為陽，陰陽消長而四時成，則凡日月之運行、星辰之躔次，皆二者之為也。陰陽成象以立天道，自此之外无他道焉。形於下者為地，不徒附乎氣而已也。其為均為母之中，必有道以發育乎萬物，是地之所以立也，而剛柔盡之矣。盖順而為柔，健而為剛，剛柔交錯而四維成，則凡水火之燥濕、土石之堅潤，皆二者之為也。剛柔成質以立地道，自此之外无他道焉。以至命於兩間者為人，人之所以為人，亦不徒形氣之粗而已。天之陽也，地之剛也，在人

Examiner Zhang, Academician, comments: This composition displays distinctive insight, and its language and tone are also dignified. Outstanding, outstanding!

To discuss what establishes the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—is to discuss the single principle of nature and destiny. Heaven has yin and yang; Earth has the firm and the yielding; humanity has benevolence and righteousness. These are what establish the Three Powers. Yet which of them is not an expression of the principle of nature and destiny? This principle has its great source in Heaven and Earth, and its entirety is present in us. Thus, what takes form above is Heaven, but it does not depend upon form alone. Beneath its outward manifestations as the round and as the ruler, there must be a Way that works wondrously through the myriad transformations. This is what establishes Heaven, and yin and yang encompass it fully. Stillness constitutes yin, and movement constitutes yang. Through the waxing and waning of yin and yang, the four seasons take shape. Thus, the movements of the sun and moon and the courses and positions of the stars are all the workings of these two. Yin and yang produce celestial configurations and thereby establish the Way of Heaven. Beyond these there is no other Way.

What takes form below is Earth, but it does not merely adhere to material force. Within its being the even [?] and the mother, there must be a Way that generates and nurtures the myriad things. This is what establishes Earth, and the firm and the yielding encompass it fully. Compliance constitutes the yielding, and vigor constitutes the firm. Through the interweaving of the firm and the yielding, the four quarters take shape. Thus, the dryness and wetness of water and fire, and the hardness and moisture of soil and stone, are all the workings of these two. The firm and the yielding produce material substance and thereby establish the Way of Earth. Beyond these there is no other Way.

As for those endowed with life between Heaven and Earth, these are human beings. What makes human beings human is likewise not merely the coarse substance of bodily form and material force. Heaven’s yang and Earth’s firmness, in human beings …

意者皆仁也天之陰也地之柔也在人得之則

得之則為仁，凡其為慈愛、為惻隱而有發舒之意者，皆仁也。天之陰也，地之柔也，在人得之則為義，凡其為裁制、為果斷而有收斂之意者，皆義也。以仁義而成德，配天地而成位，所以統貫乎萬善者在是，所以根抵乎萬事者在是。人道之所以立，又豈外此而有他道哉？吁！道一也，其散見雖有三才之别，而會歸同一性命之理。聖人作《易》，一順乎此理而已，夫豈有私智於其間哉？抑論之，性命之妙難知，奇偶之象易見。聖人泄天地之秘，而寄之卦爻法象之中，以前民用，顯道之功至矣。雖其仰觀俯察，若有效法於天地之為者，然揆厥所原，皆本諸一心之妙耳。蓋聖人之心，窮理盡性以至於命，統體一太極也。然則欲求之《易》者，又不可不求之聖人之心。

translation_en:
…when received by human beings, it becomes benevolence. All that takes the form of loving kindness and compassion and has an expansive tendency is benevolence. Heaven’s yin and earth’s yielding quality, when received by human beings, become righteousness. All that takes the form of judgment and restraint, resolution and decisiveness, and has a contracting tendency is righteousness. Through benevolence and righteousness, human beings perfect their virtue and establish their place alongside Heaven and Earth. Herein lies what unifies and runs through all goodness; herein lies what provides the root and foundation of all affairs. How could there be any other Way beyond these by which the human Way is established?

Ah! The Way is one. Although its diverse manifestations distinguish the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—they converge upon the same principle of nature and destiny. In making the Book of Changes, the sage simply followed this principle throughout. How could he have interposed his own private ingenuity? Furthermore, the subtleties of nature and destiny are difficult to know, whereas the images of odd and even are readily perceived. The sage disclosed the secrets of Heaven and Earth and lodged them in the patterns and images of the hexagrams and their lines, thereby guiding the people’s practical undertakings. His achievement in making the Way manifest was consummate. Although, in looking upward and examining downward, he seemed to be taking the workings of Heaven and Earth as his model, if we trace their source, all were rooted in the subtle workings of his single mind. For the sage’s mind, fathoming principle and fully realizing nature so as to reach destiny, is in its entirety one Supreme Ultimate. Thus, those who seek this in the Book of Changes must also seek it in the sage’s mind.

Wei Jiao 魏校

For the gentleman makes perfected virtue the basis of his conduct. Once his virtue is perfected and free from one-sidedness, it can also be verified in his conduct. How, then, could Gao Yao fail to identify these virtues one by one in addressing Yu? We may imagine that, when his discussion of the difficulty of judging men reached this point, he spoke as follows: “Virtue manifests itself in conduct and can assuredly be verified through particular deeds; when virtue is manifest in a person, it is wholly natural and free from one-sidedness. translation_en:
…[?] weakness? A person's cautious honesty may fall short of reverence; yet he expresses it with deference, and all his circumspection springs from manifest sincerity and respect. Has he ever leaned too far toward mere cautious honesty? A person with administrative ability may readily become arrogant; yet he exercises that ability with reverence, and a vigilant sense of caution remains in his heart whenever he acts. Has he ever leaned too far toward mere administrative competence? Those who are orderly and refined may seem leisurely and lacking in vigor; yet they are decisive without hesitation, steadfast and dependable. How well they combine docility with resolution! Those who are forthright and direct may seem stern and unapproachable; yet viewed from afar they are composed, and approached closely they are kindly. How well they combine uprightness with warmth!

There is the virtue of simplicity. Were one devoted solely to simplicity, it would amount merely to careless ease. Here, however, integrity resides within an unassuming manner, and one maintains one's own principles without following others. There is the virtue of firmness. Were one devoted solely to firmness, it would amount merely to obstinate extremism. Here, however, substantial sincerity governs vigorous decisiveness, and one holds faithfully to one's purpose. There is also the virtue of strength. If one were devoted solely to strength without loving righteousness, would this not be merely the courage of physical passion? Such a person esteems righteousness and advances boldly to fulfill his intentions; in affairs he does not comply heedlessly, but exerts himself to accord with the Way. Is this not strength joined with a love of righteousness?

Ah! When the nine virtues are enumerated, they can indeed be known by examining conduct. Yet in employing people possessed of these virtues, one also requires that the virtues be manifest in their persons without interruption. Is it not truly difficult to know people? Moreover, consider the age of Youyu: its flourishing government and transforming influence also arose from its proper way of employing people. Among the ministers at court, who did not manifest constancy in his virtues? And yet …

Nevertheless, Gao Yao placed great weight on presenting his counsels, and in what he told the Great Yu repeatedly returned to the employment of men possessing the nine virtues in carrying out official duties. 和之薰蒸也不知不識斯世允躋于大猷六合

punctuated: 不容以跡求。是故顯設於政教號令者，皆本諸躬行心得之餘，而風俗為之丕變；昭布於典章文物者，咸發之精神心術之蘊，而世道以之亨嘉。無黨無偏，斯民悉歸于皇極，四海之内，一太和之薰蒸也；不知不識，斯世允躋于大猷，六合之中，一協氣之融液也。積久而舒，精華於是乎旁達焉，孰得而掩之？蓄極而發，馨香於是乎升聞焉，孰得而遏之？由是神明至幽也，而道與之合，自有以潜孚于冥漠之際；神明莫測也，而氣與之通，自有以默契于蒼茫之表。派動之意見於昭薦之外，有不疾而速者矣；洞達之機著於肸蠁之先，有不行而至者矣。是則至治之極，而妙於感通如此，何莫而非明德以為之本與？大抵有是明德，則有是至治；有是至治，則有是馨香。故周公之訓又繼之曰：「黍稷非馨，明德惟馨。」盖至治之馨，即明德之馨之發也。苟不知明德，而欲以言至治，不可得已。成王命君陳治殷民，拳拳以「懋昭」「式時弘丕訓」為言，誠以君陳繼周
translation_en:
…cannot be sought through outward traces. Thus, whatever is visibly established in government, instruction, proclamations, and commands derives from the abundance of what one has personally practiced and inwardly understood, and customs are thereby profoundly transformed. Whatever is manifestly set forth in institutions, regulations, and cultural forms issues from the accumulated resources of spirit and mind, and the course of the world thereby becomes prosperous and good. Without faction or partiality, the people all turn to the sovereign standard; within the Four Seas, all are steeped in supreme harmony. Without conscious knowing or recognition, this age truly attains the Great Way; throughout the six directions, all are suffused with harmonious vital energy. Accumulated over time and then unfolded, its finest essence spreads everywhere: who could conceal it? Stored to the utmost and then released, its fragrance rises to be perceived above: who could arrest it? Thus, although the spirits are profoundly hidden, the Way accords with them, naturally bringing about a hidden correspondence in the realm of the unseen. Although the spirits are unfathomable, vital energy communicates with them, naturally bringing about a silent accord beyond the vast expanse. The impulse of movement [?] manifests beyond the conspicuous presentation of offerings: there is swiftness without haste. The workings of unobstructed communication become apparent before the spirits give any sign of their presence: there is arrival without travel. Such is the perfection of supreme government, and such the subtlety of its power to move and communicate with the spirits. What part of this does not have luminous virtue as its foundation?

In general, where there is such luminous virtue, there is such supreme government; where there is such supreme government, there is such fragrance. Hence the Duke of Zhou’s instruction continues: “Millet is not fragrant; luminous virtue alone is fragrant.” The fragrance of supreme government is indeed the manifestation of the fragrance of luminous virtue. If one does not understand luminous virtue, one cannot presume to speak of supreme government. When King Cheng commanded Jun Chen to govern the people of Yin, he earnestly spoke of “striving to make manifest” and “following these great and ample instructions,” truly because Jun Chen was succeeding the Duke of Zhou…

…the Duke of Zhou’s governance, one cannot dispense with the Duke of Zhou’s instructions; and in following his instructions, one likewise cannot dispense with luminous virtue. If luminous virtue can move even the spirits, how much more can it move human beings? This was indeed the profound intent of King Cheng’s written charge. Ah! punctuated: 詩人於南國在位者，美其服之有常及其容之自得。夫服之有常，可以見其節儉；容之自得，可以見其正直。究而言之，非文王之化，曷克致是哉？想昔風人之意，謂夫有侈心者必有侈服，有愧心者必有愧容。顧□南方之國，布列在位之臣，覲我文王之耿光也久，感我文王之美化也深。即其服，可以占其德；即其容，可以驗其中。彼燕居之服，非不能致美乎狐貉之華也，顧惟製以羔羊之皮而已。豈不曰：「此但以適體，何汰靡之足尚焉？」彼羔裘之飾，非不能致美乎三英之粲也，顧惟紃以素絲五總而已。豈不曰：「此但以飾裘，何藻麗之足崇？」故服順其制，而其用也有常；飾稱其服，而其儀也不忒。此其節儉之彰諸身者，不宛然文王卑服之模範乎？然不惟如是可以見其節儉而已。其服斯服而退食于家，歸自公門也，但見雍容於燕閒之地，其容也舒，其色也愉，委蛇委蛇，泰然而自如也；優游於居息之時，其體也胖，其神也怡，委蛇委蛇，油然而自適
translation_en:
The poet praises those holding office in the southern states for the constancy of their dress and the ease of their bearing. Constancy in dress reveals their frugality; ease of bearing reveals their uprightness. Ultimately, without King Wen’s transforming influence, how could this have been achieved? We may imagine that the poet of old meant that those with extravagant hearts inevitably wear extravagant clothes, and those with guilty hearts inevitably have shamefaced expressions. Yet [?], in the southern states, the assembled ministers holding office have long beheld the brilliant virtue of our King Wen and have been profoundly moved by his admirable transforming influence. From their clothing one can judge their virtue; from their bearing one can verify their inner character.

As for their clothes for private leisure, it is not that they could not make them beautiful with splendid fox or raccoon-dog fur. Yet they have them made only of lambskin. Is it not as though they were saying, “These are simply to make the body comfortable; what is there to esteem in extravagance?” As for the ornamentation of their lambskin coats, it is not that they could not make it beautiful with the brilliance of three ornaments. Yet they use only braided white silk in five bundles. Is it not as though they were saying, “This is simply to ornament the coat; what is there to exalt in elaborate finery?” Thus their clothing conforms to its prescribed form, and its use is constant; their ornaments suit their clothing, and their deportment is faultless. Is not this frugality, manifest in their persons, the very model of King Wen’s modest dress?

Yet this reveals more than their frugality alone. Wearing these clothes, they withdraw to eat at home, returning from the gates of public office. We see them composed and gracious in their place of leisure: their expressions relaxed, their countenances cheerful, at ease, at ease, serene and unrestrained. Resting at home, they pass their time at leisure: their bodies at ease, their spirits content, at ease, at ease, naturally comfortable within themselves…

translation_en:
…In his every movement and moment of stillness, what trace is there of violence or arrogance? In his every bow and raising of the head, what burden is there of shame? Does not the uprightness thus manifested outwardly vividly embody King Wen’s reverent bearing? Thus, if even his private dress follows a constant standard, we may know that his public dress does so as well; if even in private life he is at ease, we may know that he is likewise at ease in public life. Such was the pervasive reach of King Wen’s sagely transforming influence!
The connection between moral transformation and government is indeed longstanding, but the impetus for changing customs and renewing the people lies with the ruler. At the end of the Shang, there were exotic skills and extravagant craftsmanship, dissipation, indolence, and irreverence; the people had become morally lax. When King Wen arose, their customs changed and returned to simplicity. As wind moves things and sound elicits an echo, such effects occur naturally without being deliberately sought. The poet first discerned this in bearing and dress, and delighted in speaking of it in this way. Even after a thousand years, we can envision the moral transformation celebrated in the Two Nan sections of the Book of Odes.
“The gracious and kindly gentleman serves as the guiding cord for the four quarters.”
Zhang Song.

美純德之君統天下之大夫。天下未易統，德盛不難統也。康公所以望於成王者有在矣。想夫飄風自南之時，優游卷阿之上，君也來歌，臣也遂歌。先以壽考福祿，繼以賢德輔翼，至此其意若曰：上有仁君，則下有仁民，彼此報答之如響如聲；君有順德，則民有順志，上下感應之如風如草。吾君賢得乎？馮翼孝德，以引以翼矣。吾君德成乎？顒卬圭璋，令聞令望矣。恭已南面，孰非温良純粹之充溢？仰之有春，望之有日，何豈弟乎君子也！游歌卷阿，孰非孝弟慈祥之呈露？望之見父，親之見母，何豈弟乎君子也！天道在上，天下陶囿於覆育之中，何由而有携貳之心？親道在上，天下綜括於生鞠之内，何由而有二三
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Fu, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent, comments: “The Poetry is upright yet richly adorned; it differs from other interpretations that merely weave together the commentaries and annotations. This essay fully grasps that meaning, and so I have selected it.”
Examiner Yang, Academician, comments: “Unlike other compositions.”
Examiner Zhang, Academician, comments: “It seems extraordinary, yet is not contrived; every sentence has its proper, authentic character.”
The poem praises a ruler of pure virtue who unites the great officers of All-under-Heaven. All-under-Heaven is not easily united, but when virtue flourishes, uniting it is not difficult. Duke Kang had good grounds for placing such hopes in King Cheng. Imagine the time when the whirlwind blew from the south and they wandered at ease upon the winding hill: the ruler came singing, and his minister sang in response. First came wishes for long life, blessings, and emoluments; next came worthy and virtuous men to assist him. At this point the meaning is as though he said: When there is a benevolent ruler above, there are benevolent people below; their reciprocal responses are like sound and echo. When the ruler possesses harmonious virtue, the people have compliant intentions; the response between those above and below is like that between wind and grass. Has our ruler secured worthy men? They provide support and possess filial virtue, guiding and assisting him. Has our ruler perfected his virtue? Majestic and dignified, like the gui and zhang jade tablets, he enjoys an excellent reputation and high esteem. As he holds himself reverently and faces south to rule, what is there that does not overflow with gentleness, goodness, and purity? Looking up to him, one finds spring; gazing toward him, one finds the sun. How joyous and gracious is this lord! As he wanders and sings upon the winding hill, what is there that does not reveal filial devotion, brotherly respect, kindness, and benevolence? Looking toward him, one sees a father; drawing close to him, one sees a mother. How joyous and gracious is this lord! With the Way of Heaven above, all beneath Heaven are shaped and embraced within its sheltering nurture. How could they harbor thoughts of estrangement or divided allegiance? With the parental Way above, all beneath Heaven are gathered within its life-giving care. How could there be any wavering …

之德芒芒禹方不知其遠之至也我以為遠彼
以為近在在恃以聨屬焉而不敢跳越於一統
之外蕩蕩堯封不知其迥之甚也吾以為迥彼
以為邇人人賴以維持焉而不敢出入於大範

translation_en:
…divided allegiance. Across the boundless lands of Yu, the people do not perceive how immensely distant they are. I regard them as distant; they regard themselves as near. Everywhere they rely upon this to remain joined together and dare not leap beyond the bounds of unified rule. Throughout the vast dominions of Yao, the people do not perceive how exceedingly remote they are. I regard them as remote; they regard themselves as close. Everyone relies upon this for support and dares not stray beyond the great norms. Its strands are mine alone to direct [?]; how could there be separation without reunion? The myriad states form one family: here is the object of their love and their reverence. The myriad people share one virtue: here is the object of their attachment and their awe. Thus we know that a ruler of such pure virtue brings about a transformation of equally pure virtue. In its subtle aspect, virtue is complete within one person; in its great aspect, ordered government unites all under Heaven. Such indeed are the benefits of supporting and assisting filial virtue! Surely the abundance of long life, blessings, and emoluments proceeds from this!
Moreover, Duke Kang may truly be said to have excelled at enlightening his ruler. Amid the pleasure of excursions and song, he first stirred the ruler’s desire for long life, blessings, and emoluments, then gradually explained how to attain them, ultimately making everything depend upon obtaining worthy men. The implication that these blessings cannot be attained without obtaining worthy men is plainly apparent beyond the words themselves. If King Cheng could indeed ponder this deeply and grasp it for himself, could he possibly cease his efforts to seek worthy men, with numerous carriages and well-trained horses? The poem “The Winding Mound” (Juan a) provides a method of admonishing rulers for ten thousand generations.
Spring and Autumn Annals
“The duke watched fish at Tang.” 〔Fifth year of Duke Yin〕
Cai Chao
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Director: “The topic of watching fish truly concerns the Way of the ruler…”

…Once his inclination toward idle excursions became unrestrained, the government of the state fell into neglect; once he indulged his desires, he would no longer accept loyal remonstrance. He had surely heard the admonition against conduct outside the proper norms, yet he hurried on, foreshadowing disaster. What did the duke possess of that principle called governing the mind through ritual propriety? He himself knew that his conduct violated propriety, yet offered inspecting the territory as his excuse. The description “rejecting remonstrance and disguising wrongdoing” truly applied to him. Here the Spring and Autumn Annals specifically records, “The duke watched fishing at Tang,” to censure him. “Watched fishing” expresses disapproval of what he did; “at Tang” expresses disapproval of where he went. In this single statement, the duke’s misconduct is laid bare. How stern are the standards of the Spring and Autumn Annals!
Consider what Bo Yi told Shun: “Do not wander in idleness; do not indulge excessively in pleasure.” The Duke of Zhou likewise told King Cheng: “Do not indulge excessively in sightseeing, in idleness, in excursions, or in hunting.” Among the sages and worthies of antiquity, none failed to warn against ease and pleasure. Xibo’s remonstrance thus carried forward Bo Yi’s teachings and the house rules of the Duke of Zhou. Duke Yin approved of it in his heart but could not heed it; afterward, he merely recognized that Xibo had left behind cause for regret. This is what is meant by being comfortable amid danger and finding advantage in calamity. As for the disaster at Zhongwu, how could he … [?]

To transgress ritual propriety in order to fortify a private town was the harmful consequence of Lu’s employing hereditary ministers; to dismantle a private town in accordance with ritual propriety was the result of an eminent state’s [?] employing a sage. Fei was the Ji lineage’s private town: why, then, was it fortified? Ji Su monopolized power in Lu, and a crowd of petty men flattered him. Without cause they burdened the people, recklessly undertaking this work, and thus Fei was fortified. To say that it was fortified means that the ministerial house possessed stores of armor and weapons, and that the town enjoyed the defenses of walls and moats. Such was their transgression of ritual propriety and disregard for due limits. When Wenzi served as chief minister, his concubines did not wear silk and his horses did not eat grain: he was one upon whom the state of Lu could rely. 弱也。其萌實見於此，《春秋》直以城費書，而襄公之用人可知矣。城費，季氏之志也，孰從而墮之？盖孔子為政，行乎季孫，不怒而威，不言而信，而費以墮焉。謂之墮，則甲兵之藏廢于家也，城池之固廢于邑也。其以禮為國，有如此者。夫宿既城費，政專其手，賦半其家，此魯國之所惡也。孔子得政而遂革之，其故何哉？盖定公能用真儒，自無敵耳。向使孔子不因見用而小試，欲為此，誰用其命邪？若得遂行其志，吾知風行草偃，動無不化，滅國將可興也，絕世將可繼也。其機實在於此，《春秋》直以墮費書，而定公之用人可知矣。
噫！用非其人，則其禍不召而至；用得其人，則其效不疾而速。為人君者，可不知所鑒也哉？雖然，世卿不可用，固也；然伊陟復相太戊，丁公繼掌兵權，又何為者邪？惟其賢與公耳，可以世疑之乎？獨恨定公有聖人而弗究于用，卒使當時不見先王之化，而日入于弊。千載而下，猶可太息。
translation_en:
…weaker. The first signs of this were already apparent here. The Spring and Autumn Annals simply records the fortification of Bi, and Duke Xiang’s choice of men for office can thereby be understood. Fortifying Bi was the intention of the Ji clan; who, then, brought about the demolition of its walls? When Confucius administered the government, his authority prevailed with Jisun: he inspired awe without anger and trust without words, and thus Bi’s walls were demolished. To speak of their demolition means that the household’s stock of arms and armor was abolished and the settlement’s defensive walls and moat were rendered useless. Such was his government of the state through ritual propriety. Once Su had fortified Bi, he monopolized political power, and half the levies went to his household. This was what the state of Lu resented. Yet when Confucius gained power, he promptly reformed it. Why was this? Duke Ding could employ a true Confucian, who was naturally without an opponent. Had Confucius not been employed and given a small opportunity to prove himself, who would have obeyed his commands if he had wished to do this? Had he been allowed to carry out his intentions fully, I know that, as grass bends before the wind, every action of his would have brought transformation. Extinguished states could have been restored, and severed hereditary lines could have been continued. The possibility truly lay here. The Spring and Autumn Annals simply records the demolition of Bi’s walls, and Duke Ding’s choice of men for office can thereby be understood.
Alas! If one employs the wrong men, calamity arrives unbidden; if one employs the right men, results come swiftly without haste. Can a ruler fail to recognize the lesson to be drawn? Even so, granted that hereditary ministers should not be employed, what are we to make of Yi Zhi again serving as chief minister to Taiwu, and Duke Ding succeeding to military command? It was solely a matter of their worthiness and impartiality. Could their hereditary succession justify doubting them? My sole regret is that Duke Ding had a sage at his disposal but failed to make full use of him. Consequently, the people of that age never witnessed the transforming influence of the former kings, and conditions deteriorated daily. Even a thousand years later, one may still heave a deep sigh.

…and cannot be concealed. Does not movement account for one of these two aspects? Speaking of stillness, [an illegible character] the culmination of movement: things are gathered in autumn and stored in winter. A stern, searching force [?] brings the myriad things into completed form with solemn restraint; the power of severity and cold gathers all kinds of beings to return to their allotted destiny. They are orderly and admit no disorder, still and admit no contravention. Does not stillness account for the other aspect? Thus Heaven covers above and Earth bears below. In their alternating departure and return, they conduct the great transformation with constancy: there is either the stillness of yin or the movement of yang. Heaven bestows at the beginning, and Earth receives at the end. Through alternating opening and closing, they complete the work of the year without error: there is either the movement of yang or the stillness of yin. Throughout all ages, these are the same Heaven and Earth, and this is the same movement and stillness. As they cycle between Heaven and Earth, could anything lie outside them? For all things, these are Heaven and Earth; for all things, this is movement and stillness. They fill the space within: could anything surpass them? Ah! Such is the wondrous operation of creation and transformation, and the accomplished work of ritual and music accords with it. It is fitting that the sage should clearly set this forth to show others.
Yet I have also examined this further. Before ritual and music were instituted, the sage’s wondrous efficacy was hidden in Heaven and Earth; once ritual and music were instituted, the wondrous efficacy of Heaven and Earth resided in the sage. In Heaven and Earth, it displays the achievement of making and instituting; in the sage, it accords with the Way of generating and completing. In their mutual relation as substance and function, they have never been two separate things. Yet one must establish the supreme standard of equilibrium and harmony and be worthy of it; only then can one shoulder great responsibilities and accomplish great achievements. Otherwise, one would be unable even to do anything about ritual and music, much less Heaven and Earth. Those who aspire to restore ancient ritual and transform present-day music should understand the foundation on which to proceed.

The sun, as the essence of yang, shines by day; the moon, as the essence of yin, shines by night: they illuminate things. Were there anything they did not illuminate, they too would lack impartiality. Yet throughout the utmost extent of Heaven’s covering and Earth’s support, nothing is omitted. Those Three Kings looked upward and examined below, fully comprehending the subtleties of the patterns and images to be emulated. Opening the way for their successors and carrying on the work of their predecessors, they labored diligently to govern all within the seas. In honoring Heaven’s impartiality, they extended their all-encompassing benevolence, sheltering the myriad things beneath it: could anything fail to fulfill its life? In honoring Earth’s impartiality, they enlarged their capacity to embrace and contain, bringing the myriad things within it: could anything fail to find its proper place? In honoring the impartiality of the sun and moon, their illumination reached throughout the Four Seas without omission, and their understanding encompassed the myriad things without error: could anything conceal its true circumstances?
Thus, by sheltering what Heaven shelters, the Three Kings acted as Heaven, and impartiality was no longer Heaven’s alone. By supporting what Earth supports, the Three Kings acted as Earth, and impartiality was no longer Earth’s alone. 考試官學士楊批：性理之學，非有的見者
translation_en:
…Why, then, do his words seem different? Heaven and earth, in their constant disposition, embrace all things without deliberate intention; the sage, in his constant disposition, accords with all affairs without partial feeling. In their utmost impartiality they are one and the same. Why should he need first to take them as models and then uphold them? Only a sage can understand a sage; even the worthy cannot attain to this. The Changes reveals the subtlety of the sage’s fundamental being, whereas here Confucius speaks in terms accessible to Zixia. There was good reason for Zixia’s promptly accepting the instruction!
Second Session
Discourse
“Equilibrium Is the Great Foundation of All under Heaven”
Dong Qi 董玘
