translation_en:
…cannot speak of it; without literary power, one cannot express it fully. This paper grasps principle with precision and depth and gives it expression in clear, fluent argument, as though speaking face to face with another person—refreshing and pleasant to hear.
Examiner Zhang, Academician, comments: The learning of principle is difficult to discuss. Those accustomed merely to repeating what they hear readily produce hundreds of words, disjointed and tiresome. This composition reveals clear insight, and its language adequately expresses that insight. Its author is a man of accumulated learning.
The single principle is an undivided whole, and all transformations issue from it. This is why those who embody the Way prize establishing its foundation. Why is this? The Way originates in Heaven and is fully present in the mind; it lies within human nature and manifests itself in the feelings. Before the feelings arise, there is simply human nature, an undivided whole centered within, without the slightest deviation or inclination. The constant norms of human relationships, what is fitting in all affairs, and the principles of Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things are all encompassed here. This is the foundation of all transformations. If the gentleman can fully attain this equilibrium and establish its foundation, the substance of the Way will be complete, and wherever it manifests itself among the myriad things, it will accord with equilibrium. If, however, he does not know how to nurture it in emptiness and stillness, but merely exercises restraint in outward actions in the hope of bringing them into accord with equilibrium, then the great foundation has already collapsed, and all transformations have no source from which to issue. However diligently he considers them and however thoroughly he discusses them, in practical application he will suddenly and unwittingly fall into the deviations of excess or insufficiency. How, then, could he embody the Way of all under Heaven? When Master Zisi composed the Doctrine of the Mean, he placed the great foundation at the outset to instruct those who would embody the Way. Truly, he may be said to have carried forward the transmission of the succession of the Way…

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
者矣今夫道之在天下其端始於夫婦之
所能知能行其極至於聖人之所不能盡
其大際乎天而蟠乎地其遠橫乎四海其
小入於絲髮其顯形於鳶飛魚躍浩乎其
無窮茫乎其莫測也然析之雖散於萬殊
而斂之不外乎吾心其用雖極其廣而其
體則一而無二所謂體者何也中也性之
德也出於天而命於吾心者也是所謂天
下之大本也然何以見之亦觀諸天之道
===
===
而已矣蓋上天之載無聲無臭而萬象森
然已具凡日月之所以明四時之所以行
江河之所以流萬物之所以蕃且育者舉
於是乎出焉故曰小德川流大德敦化惟
之在人即所謂大德也而天下之道有不
由是而出者乎是故心統乎性性發為情
方其物之未接情之未發也不見所可好
而何有於喜不見所可憎而何有於怒不
見所可欣戚而何有於哀樂此所謂人生

punctuated: 者矣。今夫道之在天下，其端始於夫婦之所能知能行，其極至於聖人之所不能盡。其大際乎天而蟠乎地，其遠橫乎四海，其小入於絲髮，其顯形於鳶飛魚躍，浩乎其無窮，茫乎其莫測也。然析之雖散於萬殊，而斂之不外乎吾心；其用雖極其廣，而其體則一而無二。所謂體者何也？中也，性之德也，出於天而命於吾心者也。是所謂天下之大本也。然何以見之？亦觀諸天之道而已矣。蓋上天之載，無聲無臭，而萬象森然已具。凡日月之所以明，四時之所以行，江河之所以流，萬物之所以蕃且育者，舉於是乎出焉。故曰：「小德川流，大德敦化。」惟之在人，即所謂大德也，而天下之道有不由是而出者乎？是故心統乎性，性發為情。方其物之未接、情之未發也，不見所可好，而何有於喜？不見所可憎，而何有於怒？不見所可欣戚，而何有於哀樂？此所謂人生
translation_en:
…one who could carry forward the transmission of the succession of the Way. Now, as the Way exists throughout the world, its beginnings lie in what ordinary husbands and wives can know and practice, while its utmost reaches extend beyond what even sages can fully comprehend. In its greatness it reaches Heaven and encompasses Earth; in its remoteness it extends across the Four Seas; in its minuteness it penetrates silk threads and hairs; in its visible manifestations it appears in kites flying and fish leaping. Vast indeed is its boundlessness, immeasurable its unfathomable depth! Yet, analyzed, though it is dispersed among myriad distinctions, gathered together it does not lie outside our own minds. Though its functioning is supremely extensive, its underlying substance is one, without any second. What is meant by this underlying substance? It is centrality: the virtue of human nature, issuing from Heaven and ordained within our minds. This is what is called the great root of all under Heaven. But how can we discern it? Simply by observing the Way of Heaven.

For the workings of Heaven above have neither sound nor smell, yet the myriad forms are already present in ordered profusion. Everything whereby the sun and moon shine, the four seasons proceed, rivers flow, and the myriad things multiply and grow issues from this. Thus it is said: “The lesser virtues flow like rivers; the greater virtue effects profound transformation.” Considered as present in human beings [?], this is precisely what is called the greater virtue. Could any of the Way throughout the world fail to issue from it? Thus the mind governs human nature, and human nature manifests itself as the emotions. Before contact with external things, when the emotions have not yet arisen, one sees nothing to like—how, then, could there be delight? One sees nothing to hate—how could there be anger? One sees nothing to occasion gladness or distress—how could there be sorrow or joy? This is what is meant by “When a person is born…”

於一隅退藏於密而未倚於一物渾然在

…and still: this is the nature bestowed by Heaven.” At this time, the mind is tranquil and unmoving, without inclining toward any one quarter; it withdraws into hidden depths, without leaning toward any one thing. It remains whole within, like a mirror in its case that has not yet reflected anything, like a great bell on its stand that has not yet been struck, or like standing at the center of the earth, near none of its four sides. Is this not the original substance of the mind and the utmost equilibrium under Heaven? Yet within this wholeness, nothing is left uncontained. Although joy has not yet arisen, the substance that enables joy to attain its proper measure is present here. Although anger has not yet arisen, the substance that enables anger to attain its proper measure is preserved here. Although sorrow and pleasure have not yet arisen, the substance that enables sorrow and pleasure to attain their proper measure is established here. The lock that opens onto the hundred forms of conduct has not yet been opened, yet this is indeed the foundation of them all. The mechanism of the myriad functions has not yet moved, yet this is indeed the foundation of them all.

Thus, although it has not yet taken form in the relationship between father and son, the principles of filial devotion and parental kindness issue from here. Although it has not yet taken form in the relationship between ruler and minister, the principles of benevolence and reverence issue from here. Although it has not yet been put to use between husband and wife, applied among brothers, or extended to friends, the principles of righteousness, compliance, order, and distinction issue from here. Even in matters as slight as a single movement or moment of stillness, as minute as a meal or a breath, their principles all issue from this. The principles governing proper conduct in wealth and honor, poverty and low status, among the Yi and Di peoples, or amid hardship and adversity are all fully present here. title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
鬼神散而萬物其理無一而不蘊於此也
譬如木之引根于土雖未萌芽也而千枝
萬葉之條達者實自此而發譬如水之出
源於山雖未流行也而千流萬派之不息
者實自是而分伊尹所謂一德孔子所謂
同歸一致孟子所謂萬物皆備於我周子
所謂無極而太極程子所謂天下無性外
之物皆謂此也故曰中者天下之大本蓋
天之所命而我之所受者其用本如是其
===
大其體本如是其全不以古今而有同異
不以知愚而有加損者也然形生知發五
性感物而動動則喜怒哀樂之情見矣苟
非存養於未發之時以立其大本吾見物
至知知其感於人者無窮而喜怒哀樂其
發于我者無節天理昧而情欲勝其不物
至而人化物者幾希矣而況能行天下之
達道哉此君子之學所以貴於致中也誠
能主敬以直其内無欲以養其體雖目所

translation_en:
…ghosts and spirits in their hiddenness, and the myriad things in their multiplicity: there is not one whose principle is not contained here. It is like a tree extending its roots into the soil: although it has not yet sprouted, the spreading growth of its thousand branches and myriad leaves truly issues from this. It is like water issuing from its source in the mountains: although it has not yet begun to flow, its thousand streams and myriad unceasing tributaries truly branch out from this. What Yi Yin called “the one virtue,” what Confucius called “the same destination and a single end,” what Mencius called “the myriad things are all complete within me,” what Master Zhou called “the Ultimateless and yet the Supreme Ultimate,” and what Master Cheng called “there is nothing under Heaven outside the nature”—all refer to this. Thus it is said: “Equilibrium is the great foundation of all under Heaven.” For what Heaven ordains and we receive is inherently so vast in its functioning and so complete in its substance. It does not differ between antiquity and the present, nor is it increased or diminished according to whether one is wise or foolish.
Yet once bodily form comes into being and awareness emerges, the five aspects of the nature are stirred into activity by contact with things. With this activity, the feelings of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure appear. Unless one preserves and nurtures oneself before these feelings arise, thereby establishing the great foundation, I foresee that, as things arrive and awareness apprehends them, their stimulation of a person will be inexhaustible, while the joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure arising within oneself will lack due measure. Heaven’s principle will be obscured and emotional desires will prevail. Rare indeed will be those who, when things arrive, do not become transformed into things themselves. Zisi, fearing that the succession in the transmission of the Way would be lost, composed the Doctrine of the Mean. By speaking first of the great foundation, he intended both to illuminate the source of the great Way and to rectify people’s minds and refute heterodox teachings. For what we call human nature contains all principles within its undifferentiated stillness, where nothing has yet shown any trace. Before it responds to things, it is not temporally prior; after it responds, it is not temporally subsequent. But Laozi’s nonbeing and the Buddhists’ emptiness mean that within vacuity and stillness there is not a single thing. …those who established teachings? The principle underlying joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure before they arise lies stored within the heart. It has not yet stirred in one's thoughts or become manifest in one's limbs and actions. Other people cannot know it; spirits cannot peer into it. Utterly still and unmoving, it nevertheless penetrates the affairs of all under Heaven; only then does its principle become manifest. Is what has not yet arisen, then, what is called the formless? Are the affairs of all under Heaven what is called the formed? Within that formlessness, consider everything that exists under Heaven and that which gives existing things their existence; consider the refined and coarse aspects of all affairs under Heaven and that which makes the refined refined and the coarse coarse; consider the great and small among all things under Heaven and that which makes the great great and the small small. Do not all their principles originate here, without going beyond this [?]? Only through this does the gentleman understand that human beings are supremely noble and the heart supremely numinous, that learning is supremely concise and the Way supremely comprehensive. Here is the utmost nonbeing, yet the utmost being; the utmost emptiness, yet the utmost fullness; the utmost stillness, yet the utmost movement; the utmost proximity, yet the utmost spiritual wonder.
Master Zisi said: “Before joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure arise, this is called equilibrium. Equilibrium is the great foundation of all under Heaven.” I have often marveled at Master Zisi's skill in establishing teachings. Yet I have also marveled at the depth of his concern and the urgency of his words. Why do I say this? Master Liu said: “The people receive the equilibrium of Heaven and Earth and thereby come into life.” When human beings first came into existence, they lived amid the thick growth of plants and trees, together with deer and swine …

人不適逸也武王之時有建極之名極亦
中也以有商之人力行無度也羣聖人者
作其言中言極皆未嘗即天下之有而推
===
本之也蓋其驟之也周公而下其說長孔
子之言性與天道不可得而聞也孔子之
後七十子者離喪而莫存微言將絕異端
將起而大義將乖子思子者獨後時而孤
立於天下逆知天下後世將有為虛無之
說者矣將有為寂滅之說者矣將有為權
謀術數記誦詞章之說者矣為虛無寂滅
者高天下之中於無者也為權謀術數記
誦詞章者卑天下之中於有者也故其言
punctuated: 狃然，不識不知，順帝之則焉，則亦宜若無待於有言矣，不可得而知也。及堯之時，黎民猶有待於於變，民始有不中者矣。堯於是乎有允執厥中之名。及舜之時，始有人心惟危、道心惟微者矣。舜於是乎有精一執中之名。湯之時有建中之名，以有夏之人不適逸也。武王之時有建極之名，極亦中也，以有商之人力行無度也。羣聖人者作，其言中、言極，皆未嘗即天下之有而推本之也，蓋其繫之也。周公而下，其說長。孔子之言性與天道，不可得而聞也。孔子之後，七十子者離喪而莫存，微言將絕，異端將起，而大義將乖。子思子者獨後時而孤立於天下，逆知天下後世將有為虛無之說者矣，將有為寂滅之說者矣，將有為權謀術數、記誦詞章之說者矣。為虛無寂滅者，高天下之中於無者也；為權謀術數、記誦詞章者，卑天下之中於有者也。故其言
translation_en:
…in an untamed state [?], without conscious understanding or knowledge, they followed the rules of the Lord on High. It would thus seem that they had no need of verbal teaching; yet this cannot be known for certain. By Yao’s time, the common people still awaited transformation into harmony, and some among them had begun to depart from the Mean. Thus, with Yao came the expression “truly hold fast to the Mean.” By Shun’s time, there had begun to be the condition described as “the human mind is precarious; the mind of the Way is subtle.” Thus, with Shun came the expression “be discerning and single-minded, and hold fast to the Mean.” In Tang’s time there was the expression “establish the Mean,” because the people of Xia did not advance toward ease. In King Wu’s time there was the expression “establish the supreme standard”—the standard, too, is the Mean—because the people of Shang exerted themselves without restraint. As these sages arose, when they spoke of the Mean or the supreme standard, they never traced it back to its root by starting from the existing things of the world; this, presumably, was what they attached it to [?]. From the Duke of Zhou onward, the exposition grew extensive. Confucius’s words concerning human nature and the Way of Heaven could not be heard.

After Confucius, the seventy disciples scattered and died, until none remained. His subtle teachings were about to disappear, heterodox doctrines were about to arise, and the great principles were about to be distorted. Master Zisi alone, born in a later age and standing solitary in the world, foresaw that later generations would produce advocates of emptiness and nonbeing, advocates of quiescent extinction, and advocates of strategic scheming and manipulative techniques, memorization and literary composition. Those who advocated emptiness, nonbeing, and quiescent extinction elevated the Mean of the world into nonbeing; those who advocated strategic scheming and manipulative techniques, memorization and literary composition lowered the Mean of the world into being. title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
中也必放諸天下之有使知吾之所謂中
非淪於無也其言天下之故也必本諸無
形之中使知吾之所謂理非滯於有也夫
理一而已矣自其太虛無形者謂之天自
其賦予萬物者謂之命自其合虛與氣者
謂之心自其具於心者謂之性自其性之
未發而不偏者謂之中中非有形也以中
而名其不偏也以其不可名而名之也故
其未發於喜喜之理具於中而無所偏於
===
喜也而凡天下之喜之理由是出焉其未
發於怒怒之理具於中而無所偏於怒也
而凡天下之怒之理由是出焉未發於哀
樂哀樂之理具於中而無所偏於哀樂也
而凡天下之哀樂之理由是出焉夫喜之
理出焉則凡陽以舒之賞以勸之以至天
地之雨潤庶草之蕃廡之理皆舉之矣怒
之理出焉則凡陰以慘之罰以懲之以至
天下之雷行六極之威用之理皆舉之矣

punctuated: 中也，必放諸天下之有，使知吾之所謂中，非淪於無也。其言天下之故也，必本諸無形之中，使知吾之所謂理，非滯於有也。夫理一而已矣。自其太虛無形者謂之天，自其賦予萬物者謂之命，自其合虛與氣者謂之心，自其具於心者謂之性，自其性之未發而不偏者謂之中。中非有形也，以中而名其不偏也，以其不可名而名之也。故其未發於喜，喜之理具於中，而無所偏於喜也，而凡天下之喜之理由是出焉。其未發於怒，怒之理具於中，而無所偏於怒也，而凡天下之怒之理由是出焉。未發於哀樂，哀樂之理具於中，而無所偏於哀樂也，而凡天下之哀樂之理由是出焉。夫喜之理出焉，則凡陽以舒之，賞以勸之，以至天地之雨潤、庶草之蕃廡之理，皆舉之矣。怒之理出焉，則凡陰以慘之，罰以懲之，以至天下之雷行、六極之威用之理，皆舉之矣。
translation_en: …of equilibrium, he must extend his account to all that exists under Heaven, so that people understand that what he calls equilibrium does not sink into nothingness. When speaking of the workings of the world, he must root his account in formless equilibrium, so that people understand that what he calls principle is not confined to existent things. Principle is but one. In its aspect as the Great Void, without form, it is called Heaven; in its bestowal upon the myriad things, it is called the mandate; in its union of the void and material force (qi), it is called the mind; as present within the mind, it is called human nature; and as human nature before it is aroused, inclining to no side, it is called equilibrium. Equilibrium has no form. The word “equilibrium” names its freedom from partiality: it gives a name to what cannot be named. Thus, before joy is aroused, the principle of joy is fully present in equilibrium, without any inclination toward joy; from this emerge all the principles of joy in the world. Before anger is aroused, the principle of anger is fully present in equilibrium, without any inclination toward anger; from this emerge all the principles of anger in the world. Before sorrow and pleasure are aroused, their principles are fully present in equilibrium, without any inclination toward sorrow or pleasure; from this emerge all the principles of sorrow and pleasure in the world. When the principle of joy emerges, it encompasses all the principles by which yang brings ease and rewards provide encouragement, extending even to the nourishing rain of Heaven and Earth and the luxuriant growth of the many grasses. When the principle of anger emerges, it encompasses all the principles by which yin brings severity and punishments chastise, extending even to thunder moving through the world and the fearsome operation of the six extreme afflictions.

…what the school of Confucius calls the One; what Master Zhou calls the Limitless and sincerity; what Master Cheng calls expansiveness and complete impartiality; and what Master Zhang means by saying that emptiness is the source of humaneness—all are this same thing. The gentleman embodies it in this way, and therefore remains watchful and cautious about what he does not see, apprehensive about what he does not hear. I have ventured to understand the explanation as follows: not forgetting is called vigilance; not growing negligent is called caution; not becoming unrestrained is called apprehensiveness. Yet excessive rigidity in self-restraint forces and distorts it [?]. Mengzi says: “One must continually attend to it without anticipating results; the mind must neither forget it nor help it grow.” This is the method for preserving it. One must never presume to interfere with it through human effort and thereby distort what is natural in it. The emptiness, nonbeing, stillness, and extinction advocated by the Buddhists and Daoists rise above the mean and lack substance, submerging the world in nonbeing. The expedient schemes and techniques of Guan Zhong and Shang Yang, and the memorization and literary composition of the Han Confucians, fall below the mean and lack usefulness, leaving the world mired in being. Only then does one understand Zisi’s skill in formulating his teaching, the depth of his concern, and the far-reaching scope of his deliberation.

Your servant Zhen, trembling with fear, trembling with fear, knocks his head to the ground, knocks his head to the ground.
I humbly consider that a ruler should regard his ministers as parts of a single body: the hands and feet, in relation to the belly and heart, ultimately serve one purpose. Those skilled in offering counsel must understand the affairs of their age; those skilled in governing value a thorough understanding of conditions throughout the realm. My learning lags behind the times, and my discernment falls shamefully short of foresight. Occupying a post in the Remonstrance Bureau, I constantly fear neglecting my duties. Yet I have now had the good fortune humbly to serve [〇〇〇〇: unclear text], who brilliantly possesses Yao’s cultural virtue and broadly promulgates Yu’s commands, succeeding to …

參轉對輒開局以看詳檢院封題毎因類
而編次豈惟得
臨下之簡抑以示用民之中治已極於太平

天地之大德固宜無待於贊襄罄犬馬之愚忠

punctuated:
列聖之緒，踰三紀于茲。增置諫員，妙選時望。常參轉對，輒開局以看詳；檢院封題，毎因類而編次。豈惟得臨下之簡，抑以示用民之中。治已極於太平，法可傳於後世。仰天地之大德，固宜無待於贊襄；罄犬馬之愚忠，則亦不容於緘默。敢攄一得，用裨萬分。
盖人主坐法宮之中，以風聲皷天下之動。九州四海，非指畫之可知；一日萬幾，或知慮之不及。大凡臣僚之建議，多有社稷之令猷。意見雖殊，忠悃則一。言易悅，而繹之斯貴；謀雖好，而成之為難。請據臺諫之見員，各置奏章之簿記，遠倣書識之典，近為考覈之憑。先後相仍，黜陟攸係。九重進御，即藏副於中書；兩府參知，并宣示於樞密。外以責官司之銷注，内以付史館之編摩。聖人期于有成，君子所其無逸。昔漢相條賢良
translation_en:
…the succession of the sage emperors, for more than three twelve-year cycles now. You have increased the number of remonstrance officials and carefully selected men esteemed in their day. For submissions made in rotation at regular court audiences, you invariably establish an office to examine them in detail; sealed submissions from the reviewing office [?] are arranged by category. This not only simplifies Your Majesty’s oversight of those below, but also demonstrates your application of the mean in governing the people. Government has already attained perfect peace, and its institutions can be transmitted to later generations. Looking up to your great virtue, like that of Heaven and Earth, there should surely be no need for assistance. Yet, in exhausting my humble loyalty, like that of a dog or horse, I cannot remain silent. I venture to set forth one modest insight, hoping to contribute one part in ten thousand.
The ruler sits within his palace and, through his moral influence, stirs all the world to action. The Nine Provinces and Four Seas cannot be comprehended merely by pointing and delineating; among the myriad affairs of a single day, some may lie beyond his knowledge and consideration. Proposals submitted by officials often contain excellent plans for the state. Though their opinions differ, their sincere loyalty is one. It is easy to take pleasure in words; what matters is to follow through on them. However good a plan may be, carrying it to completion is difficult. I request that a register of memorials be established for each currently serving censor and remonstrance official. This would emulate the ancient practice of written records and provide an immediate basis for assessing performance. Successive incumbents would continue the records, and demotion and promotion would depend upon them. Once a memorial has been presented to Your Majesty in the innermost palace, a duplicate should be deposited in the Secretariat. The two chief administrations should jointly take cognizance of it, and it should also be communicated to the Bureau of Military Affairs. Outside the palace, the responsible offices should be required to record its completion; within, it should be entrusted to the Historiography Office for compilation. The sage expects results to be achieved; the gentleman makes freedom from ease his abiding concern. Formerly, a Han chief minister arranged in order the worthy and good men’s…

之對，本不同時；至唐宗列忠諫之屏，亦為異代。豈若上下交儆，載聞喜起之風？庶幾宮府相符，無有壅蔽之患。月稽歲考，言必聽而諫必行。乾始坤成，德可久而業可大。臣鎮無任瞻天望聖、激切屏營之至，謹奉表陳請以聞。

第叁場
策

董玘

同考試官都給事中任批：「用人理財，正今日急務，當宁所欲聞者。此策於致弊之由與救弊之方，歷述無遺，而用世之才居然可見。得士如此，可以薦之上矣。」
translation_en:
…responses belonged to a different time; when the Tang emperor displayed loyal remonstrances on a screen, that too was in another age. How could these compare with superiors and subordinates admonishing one another, so that the spirit of joyful diligence might once again be heard? Thus may the palace and the offices of government act in accord, free from the danger of obstruction and concealment. With monthly scrutiny and annual assessment, counsel will surely be heard and remonstrance acted upon. As Heaven initiates and Earth brings to completion, virtue may endure and achievement grow great. Your servant Zhen, looking up toward Heaven and toward Your Majesty, cannot contain his intense emotion and utmost trepidation. I respectfully submit this memorial to lay my request before you.

Third Session
Policy Essays
First Question
Dong Qi 董玘

Comment by Associate Examiner Ren, Chief Supervising Secretary: “Employing men and managing finances are precisely the urgent tasks of today, matters on which His Majesty wishes to hear advice. This policy essay sets out, one by one and without omission, both the causes of abuses and the means of remedying them. Its author’s ability to serve in public affairs is plainly evident. Having obtained a scholar such as this, we may recommend him to His Majesty.”

同考試官侍讀徐批：場屋閱卷，恒以失士為懼。及得此卷，前場文字之妙，固已出人遠甚；五策尤宏博精深，出入經傳。其考論故實，如倒囊出物，不煩心力；而鋪張治體，商確時事，又雍容精練，若素習者。鑒賞之餘，不勝擊節。用人理財一策，具陳經畫大計，故特錄之，惜不能盡刻也。

制治者有一定之法，繼治者有一定之守。
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Chen, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: He possesses far-reaching insight and broad, cultivated learning; his arguments are precise and incisive, and his plans well ordered. Here one sees the Sacred Progenitor’s grand designs for governing the realm, which may be upheld unchanged for ten thousand generations.

Associate Examiner Xu, a Hanlin Reader-in-waiting, comments: When reading examination papers, I am always afraid of overlooking a worthy scholar. When I came upon this paper, the excellence of his writing in the earlier sessions already placed him far above others. His five policy essays are especially wide-ranging, precise, and profound, drawing freely upon the classics and their commentaries. His examination and discussion of historical precedents is like tipping objects out of a bag, requiring no mental exertion. His exposition of the principles of government and his weighing of current affairs are likewise poised and polished, as though these were matters long familiar to him. Beyond admiring his work, I could not help beating time in enthusiastic approval. The policy essay on employing men and managing finances fully sets out his major plans for governance, and so we have selected it for inclusion. It is a pity that we cannot print them all.

Examiner Yang, a Hanlin Academician, comments: His writing in the first two sessions is powerful, profound, elegant, and vigorous. His talent flows abundantly, yet its sharp edge remains concealed. Having read these pieces repeatedly, I find them all worthy of inclusion. The five policy essays are equally deserving. We include this one to give an indication of the others, and also to encourage his ambition to serve the world. Those presiding over the examination may congratulate themselves on having found such a scholar.

Examiner Zhang, a Hanlin Academician, comments: All five policy essays display learning suited to serving the world, rather than merely extensive knowledge and grand language. We include this one to give a glimpse of that learning. Considered alongside his writing from the earlier sessions, all are beyond the reach of other compositions. For first place in the Metropolitan Examination, who could there be but you?

Those who establish good government have fixed methods; those who carry it forward have fixed principles to uphold.

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
事庫藏之出納有程倉廥之盈虛有數當
是時也戸部所以制天下之用者其財賦
如此而已矣未聞有公私困乏之憂馴至
今日有非前日之舊者矣以官制言之員
外之置幾倍於舊額添註之名時見於奏
請着籍者多至萬計待次者動踰十年多
方踈理用意吹毛而選法猶未得通若是
者其故何也蓋入仕之路太廣倖進之門
未塞學校以輸粟而入監文胥以納銀而
===
免役有希內降之恩賜職級不由然作缺
有藉邊鄙之令則入官不由於類選考覈
雖嚴而工宦者幸免實諸捷徑而遵化者
旁出執簿或病其太繁臨事又難於推擇
昔人所謂一官而三人守之居者一人去
者一人而伺之者又一人譬如決水於不
流之澤舊者未導新者又至填堙充塞莫
可踈通頃因天變之見而有內外考察之
令若將以損之也然不究其本而惟末之

punctuated: 事，庫藏之出納有程，倉廥之盈虛有數。當是時也，戸部所以制天下之用者，其財賦如此而已矣，未聞有公私困乏之憂。馴至今日，有非前日之舊者矣。以官制言之，員外之置幾倍於舊額，添註之名時見於奏請，着籍者多至萬計，待次者動踰十年。多方踈理，用意吹毛，而選法猶未得通。若是者，其故何也？蓋入仕之路太廣，倖進之門未塞。學校以輸粟而入監，文胥以納銀而免役。有希內降之恩，賜職級不由然作缺；有藉邊鄙之令，則入官不由於類選。考覈雖嚴，而工宦者幸免；實諸捷徑，而遵化者旁出。執簿或病其太繁，臨事又難於推擇。昔人所謂一官而三人守之，居者一人，去者一人，而伺之者又一人。譬如決水於不流之澤，舊者未導，新者又至，填堙充塞，莫可踈通。頃因天變之見，而有內外考察之令，若將以損之也。然不究其本，而惟末之
translation_en:
… affairs. Receipts and disbursements from the treasuries followed prescribed procedures, and the fullness or depletion of the granaries and storehouses was recorded in figures. At that time, these revenues alone constituted the resources with which the Ministry of Revenue regulated expenditure throughout the realm. Yet one heard no concern about hardship and want in either public or private finances. Gradually we have reached the present day, when things are no longer as they formerly were.

To speak of the official establishment, appointments beyond the authorized complement are several times the former quota. Requests for supplementary appointments repeatedly appear in memorials to the throne. Those entered on the registers number in the tens of thousands, while those awaiting their turn frequently wait more than ten years. Many methods have been employed to clear the backlog, and scrutiny has become meticulous to the point of faultfinding, yet the appointment system still cannot function smoothly. Why is this so? It is because the routes into official service are too numerous, and the gates to advancement through favor remain unclosed. Students in the schools gain entry to the Directorate of Education by contributing grain, and clerks gain exemption from service by paying silver. Some seek the favor of orders issued from within the palace, receiving offices and ranks without following the normal procedure for filling vacancies [?]; others take advantage of regulations concerning the frontier, entering office without selection by category.

Although performance evaluations are strict, those adept at maneuvering in official life escape through good fortune. The shortcuts are crowded, while those who follow the prescribed course branch off by other routes [?]. Those responsible for the registers sometimes find them excessively cumbersome, and when an appointment must actually be made, recommending and selecting a suitable person is again difficult. As people of former times put it, three men attend upon a single office: one occupies it, one leaves it, and yet another waits for it. It is like channeling water into a marsh with no outlet: before the old water has been drained, new water arrives. Everything becomes clogged and blocked, with no means of clearing a passage.

Recently, the appearance of celestial anomalies prompted an order for evaluations of officials both at court and in the provinces, seemingly with the intention of reducing their numbers. Yet, without investigating the root of the problem, attending only to its outward effects…

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
圖其可得乎或者之論謂宜體
祖宗設官之意愛惜爵賞慎重名器布公道以
杜倖進破常調以待異才不以一時之急
而行鬻爵之令不以一人之言而施內降
之恩嚴解送之選重考覈之法因事置官
而事已即罷如漢人美俗沒者直指使者
之命可也官事兼攝而冗官必省如唐人
罷斜封數千人裁冗官八百員之舉可也
萬一有以招怨為言者則曰非以招怨也
將以復職掌之舊也此則不損之損選法
庶幾其少清矣以財用言之盡民間之財
而歸之公上盡州縣之財而歸之京師常
賦不足則取之羨餘內帑不足則取之外
府竭澤以漁傷根以刈而國用猶有不足
若是者其故何也盖出之也不量其所入
積之也不充其所散民田有世業而豪強
或至於兼并軍功有冒賞而俸料遂至於
濫給內庭之供應于何而句考匠藝之餼

庶幾其少清矣以財用言之盡民閒之財
而歸之公上盡州縣之財而歸之京師常
賦不足則取之羨餘內帑不足則取之瑤
府竭澤以漁傷根以刈而國用猶有不足
若是者其故何也蓋出之也不量其所入
積之也不充其所散民田有世業而豪強
或至於兼并軍功有冒賞而俸料遂至於
濫給內庭之供應于何而句考匠藝之餼
punctuated:
圖，其可得乎？或者之論，謂宜體祖宗設官之意，愛惜爵賞，慎重名器，布公道以杜倖進，破常調以待異才。不以一時之急而行鬻爵之令，不以一人之言而施內降之恩。嚴解送之選，重考覈之法，因事置官，而事已即罷，如漢人美俗沒者、直指使者之命可也。官事兼攝，而冗官必省，如唐人罷斜封數千人、裁冗官八百員之舉可也。萬一有以招怨為言者，則曰：「非以招怨也，將以復職掌之舊也。」此則不損之損，選法庶幾其少清矣。

以財用言之，盡民間之財而歸之公上，盡州縣之財而歸之京師。常賦不足，則取之羨餘；內帑不足，則取之外府。竭澤以漁，傷根以刈，而國用猶有不足。若是者，其故何也？盖出之也，不量其所入；積之也，不充其所散。民田有世業，而豪強或至於兼并；軍功有冒賞，而俸料遂至於濫給。內庭之供應，于何而句考？匠藝之餼
translation_en:
…to devise measures—can that achieve the desired result? Some argue that we should embody the intentions of our ancestors in establishing offices, be sparing with ranks and rewards, treat titles and insignia with due gravity, uphold impartiality to block advancement through favoritism, and depart from routine procedures to accommodate exceptional talent. An urgent need of the moment should not prompt an order to sell ranks, nor should one person's words occasion favors conferred by orders issued from within the palace. Selection for forwarding candidates should be rigorous, and procedures for evaluating performance should carry weight. Offices should be established as tasks require and abolished once those tasks are completed, following the Han precedent of appointments of “meisu mozhe” [?] and investigating emissaries (zhizhi shizhe). Official duties should be combined under a single incumbent, and redundant posts must be eliminated, following the Tang measures that dismissed several thousand recipients of irregular appointments issued in slant-sealed envelopes and abolished eight hundred redundant posts. Should anyone object that this would provoke resentment, the reply should be: “The purpose is not to provoke resentment, but to restore the former allocation of official responsibilities.” This would be reduction without impairment; the system of selection might thereby become somewhat less corrupt.

As for public finances, all the people's wealth is drawn into the government's hands, and all the wealth of the prefectures and counties is drawn into the capital. When regular taxes prove insufficient, surpluses are tapped; when the palace treasury proves insufficient, the external treasuries are tapped. The marsh is drained to catch its fish, and the roots are injured in harvesting; yet state expenditure still lacks sufficient funds. Why is this so? Expenditure is not measured against revenue, and what is accumulated does not cover what is disbursed. The people's fields are hereditary holdings, yet powerful families may engross them. Rewards for military merit are claimed fraudulently, so that salaries and allowances come to be distributed indiscriminately. Where are the supplies provided to the inner court checked and audited? The provisions for artisans…

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
廩于何而會計鹽筴之利不盡給於軍旅
帑藏之積或半費於賞賚營繕則前後相
仍禱祠則寺觀相望昔人所謂事之害財
者有三一曰冗吏二曰冗兵三曰冗費三
冗未去十年之後將益耗竭譬如瀦水於
尾閭之川後者未繼前者已涸隨注隨消
無所底止頃因議臣之言而有鑄錢之令
者將以益之也然不清其源而徒塞其流
其可得乎或者之論謂宜體
===
===
祖宗制財之意慎乃儉德節以制度按往迹以
經畫考時弊以釐正與其斂怨於上孰若
藏富於下與其誅求之峻孰若賜予之節
不以有用之財為無用之費不以有涯之
積應無涯之求如王制之說則以三十年
之畊而餘九年之積可也如晁錯之說則
敺末技游手之民而歸之農可也萬一有
以掣肘為言者則曰是何掣肘也將以復
職掌之舊也此則不益之益國用庶幾其

廩于何而會計臨莢之剩否盡給於軍旅
帑藏之積或半費於賞賚營繕則前後相
仍禱祠則寺觀相望昔人所謂事之害財
者有三一曰冗吏二曰冗兵三曰冗費三
冗未去十年之後將益耗竭譬如潴水於
池閉之川後者未繼前者已涸隨注隨消
無所底當頃因議臣之言而有鑄錢之令
君將以益之也然不清其源而徒塞其流
其可得乎或者之論謂宜體
===
祖宗制財之意慎乃儉德節以制度損益遵以
經畫考耕耨以覈正與其斂然於上孰若
藏富於下與其誅求之峻孰若賜予之節
不以有用之財為無益之費不以有涯之
積應無涯之求如王制之說則以三十年
之耕而餘九年之積可也如鼂錯之說則
毆末技游手之民而歸之農可也萬一有
以掣肘為言者則曰是何掣肘也將以復
職掌之舊也此則不益之益國用庶幾其
punctuated: 廩于何而會計？鹽筴之利不盡給於軍旅，帑藏之積或半費於賞賚。營繕則前後相仍，禱祠則寺觀相望。昔人所謂事之害財者有三：一曰冗吏，二曰冗兵，三曰冗費。三冗未去，十年之後，將益耗竭。譬如瀦水於尾閭之川，後者未繼，前者已涸，隨注隨消，無所底止。頃因議臣之言而有鑄錢之令者，將以益之也。然不清其源，而徒塞其流，其可得乎？或者之論，謂宜體祖宗制財之意，慎乃儉德，節以制度，按往迹以經畫，考時弊以釐正。與其斂怨於上，孰若藏富於下？與其誅求之峻，孰若賜予之節？不以有用之財為無用之費，不以有涯之積應無涯之求。如王制之說，則以三十年之畊而餘九年之積可也；如晁錯之說，則敺末技游手之民而歸之農可也。萬一有以掣肘為言者，則曰：是何掣肘也？將以復職掌之舊也。此則不益之益，國用庶幾其
translation_en:
…and their grain allowances—how are these accounted for? The profits from the salt monopoly are not wholly devoted to the armed forces, while perhaps half the treasury’s reserves are spent on rewards and gifts. Construction and repairs follow one another without cease, and temples and monasteries where prayers are offered stand within sight of one another. As men of former times said, three things harm public finances: first, superfluous officials; second, superfluous soldiers; and third, superfluous expenditure. Unless these three excesses are eliminated, in ten years resources will be still further depleted. It is like storing water in a river that drains into the Tail Sluice: before the next water arrives, the previous water has already run dry. It disappears as fast as it pours in, without end. Recently, following a deliberating official’s proposal, an order was issued to mint coins, intending thereby to augment resources. Yet without clearing the source, merely blocking the flow—can this achieve its purpose?
Some argue that we should embody the ancestral emperors’ intentions in regulating finances, carefully uphold the virtue of frugality, and impose restraint through established institutions. We should examine past practices when making plans and investigate present abuses in order to rectify them. Rather than accumulate resentment against those above, would it not be better to preserve wealth among those below? Rather than exact resources harshly, would it not be better to exercise restraint in bestowing gifts? Useful resources should not be spent on useless expenses, nor finite reserves used to meet limitless demands. Following the teaching of “Royal Regulations” (Wangzhi), thirty years of cultivation should leave reserves sufficient for nine years. Following Chao Cuo’s teaching, those engaged in subsidiary crafts and those living in idleness should be directed back to farming. Should anyone object that this would tie their hands, we would reply: “How does this tie your hands? It merely restores the former provisions of the Duties of Offices (Zhizhang).” This, then, is an increase achieved without increasing revenues, and the state’s finances might thereby…

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
少紓矣大抵自古創業之初其立法未有
不善惟夫積習既久少變其初則流弊日
滋將有不可收拾焉者考之漢事輪臺之
悔則以變其恭儉之習也鴻都之恥則以
變其臺閣之制也至於唐宋何莫不然竊
嘗莊誦我
文皇之言曰凡開創之主其經歷多謀慮深每
作一事必籌度數日乃行亦欲子孫世守
之不忘也洋洋
===

謝丕

豈徒事佔畢焉哉歎賞

今日獻
第二問
同考試官給事中張 批〔論卷□□□□〕
諸丕
〔策辯然初二場已許其不凡五答尤見學識〕
〔豈徒事佔畢爲哉敬穆〕

少紓矣。大抵自古創業之初，其立法未有不善。惟夫積習既久，少變其初，則流弊日滋，將有不可收拾焉者。考之漢事，輪臺之悔，則以變其恭儉之習也；鴻都之恥，則以變其臺閣之制也。至於唐宋，何莫不然？竊嘗莊誦我文皇之言曰：「凡開創之主，其經歷多，謀慮深，每作一事，必籌度數日乃行，亦欲子孫世守之不忘也。」洋洋聖謨，請以為今日獻。

謝丕
同考試官給事中張批：該博，□思俊逸，采蔚然。初二場已許其不凡，五策尤見卓識，豈徒事佔畢焉哉？歎賞皇祖休烈，以致將順，此槩見之矣。尚有望子于大對。
同考試官編修劉批：五策奇偉異常，如
translation_en:
…may be somewhat eased. Generally speaking, from antiquity onward, the laws established at the founding of a dynasty have invariably been sound. Only after practices have become entrenched over time, and small departures have been made from the original arrangements, do abuses multiply daily, until they threaten to become impossible to remedy. Examining the affairs of the Han, the repentance at Luntai resulted from a departure from its habits of reverence and frugality; the disgrace of Hongdu resulted from a departure from its system of central administration. How could the Tang and Song have been any different? I have reverently recited these words of our Emperor Wen: “Every founding ruler has extensive experience and deliberates deeply. Whenever he undertakes anything, he must consider it for several days before acting. He also wishes his descendants to preserve it generation after generation without forgetting.” How abundant this sagely counsel! I beg to offer it to Your Majesty today.
Second Question
Xie Pi
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Supervising Secretary: His learning is comprehensive; his □ thought is outstanding and his literary expression richly flourishing [?]. In admiring and praising the illustrious achievements of the imperial ancestor, he seeks to support and guide the sovereign toward the good: this can broadly be seen here. I have further hopes for you in your response at the Palace Examination.

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
明珠出海光彩燁然夫人皆知為希世之珍
此篇於
聖祖君臣同遊之盛信敘無遺而
今日將順之宜尤為切中故特錄之觀者得其一固可槩其
餘矣
考試官學士楊批策能頌述我
皇祖君臣同遊之盛終篇所對徵于古而不泛宜于今而可行
且詞氣悠揚光采煥發讀之令人起敬
考試官學士張批五對超出塲屋純雅可
===
愛錄此槩見其一云
有天下之大分有天下之至情君尊臣卑
天下之大分也君臣相與天下之至情也
分之所在不患其不嚴而情之所感每病
於難合此君子小人之所由以進退而世
道盛衰之機也洪惟我
太祖高皇帝生而神明首出庶物起南服以宅
中夏屈羣策以定四方即位之後昧爽臨
朝日晏忘食虛心清問從諫如流自微言

考試官學士楊批：策能頌述我皇祖君臣同遊之盛，終篇所對，徵于古而不泛，宜于今而可行，且詞氣悠揚，光采煥發，讀之令人起敬。

translation_en:
…a luminous pearl emerging from the sea, its brilliance resplendent: everyone recognizes it as a treasure rarely encountered in the world. This essay indeed leaves nothing untold of the flourishing fellowship between the Sagely Progenitor and his ministers. It is especially apt concerning the proper ways to support and guide the sovereign today; hence its particular selection for inclusion. From this one essay, readers can surely gain an impression of the others.
Examiner Yang, Academician, comments: This policy essay fittingly celebrates the flourishing fellowship between Our Imperial Progenitor and his ministers. Throughout, its responses draw upon antiquity without becoming vague, and are appropriate to the present and practicable. Its language and spirit are flowing and expansive, its brilliance radiant; reading it inspires respect.
Examiner Zhang, Academician, comments: The five responses rise above ordinary examination writing; they are refined, elegant, and delightful. This one is included to give a representative glimpse.
There are the great distinctions of rank under Heaven, and there are the deepest affections under Heaven. The ruler’s exalted position and the minister’s subordinate position constitute the great distinctions of rank under Heaven; the fellowship of ruler and minister constitutes the deepest affections under Heaven. Where rank is concerned, there is no fear that its distinctions will lack strictness; but where feelings move people, the difficulty of achieving harmony is a frequent concern. This determines the advancement or withdrawal of gentlemen and petty men, and is the pivot upon which the flourishing or decline of the age turns. We reverently consider Our Emperor Taizu Gao: endowed from birth with divine sagacity, he stood foremost among all beings. Rising in the southern regions, he established his seat in the Central Lands; drawing upon the counsel of many, he pacified the four quarters. After ascending the throne, he held court before dawn and, late in the day, forgot to eat. With an open mind he sought enlightened counsel, accepting remonstrance as readily as water flows. title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
以至大政皆謀議之所先自公卿以至將
吏皆咨訪之所及自正朝以至便殿皆延
接之所在盖嘗莊誦
五倫一書所載而有以窺見當時
君臣同遊之盛矣如官僚之議叅之兩府藩屏
之建謀之侍臣語學士宋濂以漢治之未
盡語中丞劉基以天位之可憂南北之治
與學士劉三吾言之名將之道與都督張
温言之許存仁博士也而與之講洪範庶
===
徵之應許好問縣令也而與之論祈天永
命之道尋常答問如家人之唯諾往來詰
難如師弟子之告語雖虞廷之賡歌周人
之燕樂其交歡之情亦不過此若漢唐諸
君則有可慨者矣漢武之不快於汲黯梁
武之詰責於賀琛叚平仲錯愕於德宗之
猜忌令狐綯悚懾於宣宗之聰察此皆中
材之主以智御人無足道者乃若漢文帝
止輦受奏而賈誼顧有長沙之行唐太宗

punctuated:
以至大政，皆謀議之所先；自公卿以至將吏，皆咨訪之所及；自正朝以至便殿，皆延接之所在。盖嘗莊誦《五倫》一書所載，而有以窺見當時君臣同遊之盛矣。如官僚之議，叅之兩府；藩屏之建，謀之侍臣。語學士宋濂以漢治之未盡，語中丞劉基以天位之可憂。南北之治，與學士劉三吾言之；名將之道，與都督張温言之。許存仁，博士也，而與之講《洪範》庶徵之應；許好問，縣令也，而與之論祈天永命之道。尋常答問，如家人之唯諾；往來詰難，如師弟子之告語。雖虞廷之賡歌、周人之燕樂，其交歡之情亦不過此。
若漢唐諸君，則有可慨者矣。漢武之不快於汲黯，梁武之詰責於賀琛，叚平仲錯愕於德宗之猜忌，令狐綯悚懾於宣宗之聰察，此皆中材之主，以智御人，無足道者。乃若漢文帝止輦受奏，而賈誼顧有長沙之行，唐太宗
translation_en:
…up to major affairs of government, all were first subjected to deliberation. From the highest ministers down to military commanders and civil officials, all were consulted; from the main court to the private audience halls, all were places where he received them. I have reverently read the accounts recorded in the Five Relationships (Wulun), and through them glimpsed the flourishing fellowship between ruler and ministers at that time. For example, he consulted the two chief agencies on deliberations concerning officialdom, and sought the counsel of attendant ministers on establishing princely bulwarks of the realm. He spoke to Academician Song Lian about the shortcomings of Han government, and to Vice Censor-in-chief Liu Ji about the anxieties attending the imperial throne. He discussed the governance of north and south with Academician Liu Sanwu, and the way of an outstanding general with Chief Military Commissioner Zhang Wen. Xu Cunren was an Erudite, yet he discussed with him the correspondences of the various signs described in the “Great Plan” (Hongfan). Xu Haowen was a District Magistrate, yet he discussed with him the way to pray to Heaven for an enduring mandate. Their ordinary questions and answers were like the exchanges of a family; their challenges and rejoinders were like conversations between teacher and pupils. Even the answering songs at the court of Shun and the banquet music of the Zhou could not surpass the warmth of their mutual enjoyment.
As for the rulers of Han and Tang, there is much to lament. Emperor Wu of Han was displeased with Ji An; Emperor Wu of Liang rebuked He Chen; Duan Pingzhong was dismayed by Emperor Dezong’s suspicions; and Linghu Tao trembled before Emperor Xuanzong’s penetrating scrutiny. These were all rulers of middling ability who used cleverness to control others, and are scarcely worth discussing. But even Emperor Wen of Han, who stopped his carriage to receive memorials, nevertheless sent Jia Yi away to Changsha; and Emperor Taizong of Tang…

punctuated:
寵程名振之不屈，而晚年乃欲詰臣下之細過。十事要說，玄宗始嘉納之矣，何以不能自克於後來之侈心？侍從陳言，宋仁宗每欵接之矣，何以不能究用於天章之引對？之數君者，皆恭儉禮下，號為一時令主，而所為且如此，他尚何望焉？噫！甚矣，君臣相遇之難也！尊卑闊別，而堂陛之分嚴；禮節繁多，而手足之義薄。自非人君降志以誘之，溫顏以接之，博問以盡之，不拒人以給，不自衒以明，不以先覺為能，不以臆度為知，則為之臣者，雖有遇主于巷之忠、納約自牖之願，亦豈得從容展布，以效其所欲言者哉？
今日聖明在上，紹履慶基，恢弘大業，敬守祖宗之法，明習天下之務。邇者退朝之暇，數延羣臣，講求治理。雖入告之謀非外朝之所得聞，而晝日之接則羣臣之所共見。
translation_en:
…favored Cheng Mingzhen for his refusal to yield, yet in his later years wished to interrogate his ministers about their minor faults. Xuanzong initially welcomed and accepted the Essential Exposition of Ten Matters; why, then, could he not restrain his subsequent appetite for extravagance? Whenever his attendant officials offered advice, Emperor Renzong of Song received them cordially; why, then, could he not fully put their advice into practice when he summoned them to audience in the Tianzhang Pavilion? These several rulers [?] were all respectful and frugal, treating their subordinates with courtesy, and were acclaimed as excellent sovereigns of their times. Yet even their conduct was like this: what could one hope for from the others? Alas, how very difficult it is for ruler and ministers to achieve mutual understanding! The exalted and the lowly are far apart, and the distinction between the hall and its steps is strict; ceremonial observances multiply, while the bond that should unite them like hands and feet grows weak. Unless the ruler humbles himself to encourage his ministers, receives them with a kindly countenance, and questions them broadly to draw out all they have to say—unless he refrains from rebuffing others with verbal dexterity or flaunting his own discernment, from treating prior insight as proof of ability or conjecture as knowledge—then even ministers with the loyalty to seek their lord in a narrow lane and the wish to present a simple offering through a window could hardly set forth their thoughts freely and convey all they wished to say.
Today, Your Sagely Majesty reigns above, having inherited an auspicious foundation and enlarged the great imperial undertaking, reverently preserving the laws of your ancestors and thoroughly acquainting yourself with the affairs of the realm. Recently, in your leisure after court, you have repeatedly summoned your ministers to discuss and investigate good government. Although the counsels presented within are beyond the hearing of the outer court, these audiences in the light of day have been witnessed by all the ministers…

text:
當宁一呼聽者生氣升階一拜觀者動色傳
之天下皆欣欣然相告以為不世之遇凡
有志於用世者莫不引領企望思以仰承
德美之萬一况於愚生親承明問道之使言
而敢隱其一得之愚乎第恐迂愚之言不
足以動執事之聽耳竊嘗疑之諸臣者之
賜對幸也然頃刻相覲時或不得而久咫尺
相違言或不得而盡况所議者皆軍國之
遠謀天下之大計立談之頃不知能一一
委曲敷奏而極事理之當乎否也請
令賜對之後別具封章各陳所見或即日以
上聞或非時而請對言之必聽聽之必行無已
則如唐人之制諫官隨中書奏事以從更
大臣之直議或如宋人之規儒臣更番入
直以備
燕閒之顧問此一說也至於外服庶僚或以
受
命而廷辭或以奏計而入

punctuated: 當宁一呼，聽者生氣；升階一拜，觀者動色。傳之天下，皆欣欣然相告，以為不世之遇。凡有志於用世者，莫不引領企望，思以仰承德美之萬一。况於愚生，親承明問，道之使言，而敢隱其一得之愚乎？第恐迂愚之言，不足以動執事之聽耳。竊嘗疑之：諸臣者之賜對，幸也。然頃刻相覲，時或不得而久；咫尺相違，言或不得而盡。况所議者，皆軍國之遠謀、天下之大計，立談之頃，不知能一一委曲敷奏，而極事理之當乎否也？請令賜對之後，別具封章，各陳所見，或即日以上聞，或非時而請對。言之必聽，聽之必行。無已，則如唐人之制，諫官隨中書奏事，以從更大臣之直議；或如宋人之規，儒臣更番入直，以備燕閒之顧問。此一說也。至於外服庶僚，或以受命而廷辭，或以奏計而入
translation_en:
At a single call from the sovereign, those who hear are invigorated; at a single bow upon ascending the steps, those who watch are visibly moved. When word spreads throughout the realm, all joyfully tell one another of this opportunity scarcely encountered in an age. All who aspire to serve the world crane their necks in eager expectation, hoping to uphold even a ten-thousandth part of His Majesty’s splendid virtue. How much more, then, should an unworthy student like me, personally receiving your discerning questions and being encouraged to speak, dare conceal whatever small insight my foolishness affords? I fear only that my pedantic and foolish words will not move you who preside over this examination.

I have privately pondered a difficulty: it is fortunate for ministers to be granted an audience. Yet their meetings are brief, and there may be insufficient time to remain long; even at such close quarters, separation comes before they can finish speaking. Moreover, everything discussed concerns long-range plans for military and state affairs and great policies for the realm. In the brief span of a standing conversation, I wonder whether they can explain each matter fully in their reports to the throne and arrive at the most fitting judgment of its circumstances and principles.

I request that, after being granted an audience, they be ordered to prepare separate sealed memorials, each setting out his views, either submitting them for imperial consideration that very day or requesting an audience outside the regular times. What they say must be heard, and what is heard must be acted upon. If further measures are needed, follow the Tang system, whereby remonstrance officials accompanied the Secretariat when it reported affairs, to follow and revise the frank deliberations of the high ministers [?]; or follow the Song practice, whereby scholarly officials took turns on duty at court, ready to answer imperial inquiries during His Majesty’s leisure. This is one proposal.

translation_en:
…to attend an imperial audience, one or two should also occasionally be summoned to discuss what is appropriate to the customs of the various regions and the hardships suffered by ordinary households. This would provide an opportunity to assess the extent of their administrative achievements and their priorities in relaxing or tightening measures, and thereby to judge their abilities, the depth of their learning and understanding, and the integrity or perversity of their intentions. This is another proposal. In this way, everyone might express his views fully, and every undertaking achieve results. The worthy would have the means to distinguish themselves, while the unworthy would have nowhere to hide. Good counsel would not remain concealed, and the strength of the state would daily advance toward flourishing and enlightenment. The achievements of enlightened counsel and harmonious assistance could then be attained without toil. These include measures already put into practice by our Sagely Ancestor, and all are matters that our enlightened sovereign would gladly hear. I hope that you will select these suggestions and present them to the throne; they might make some small contribution to assisting the sovereign in his good purposes.
Third Question
Zhan Ruoshui

…the foundation, and only then can one grasp the essentials of governing All-under-Heaven; grasp those essentials, and only then can one nourish the foundation of All-under-Heaven. What is the foundation? Whether the mind is preserved or lost. What are the essentials? The employment or dismissal of men. Through the foundation one grasps the essentials, and the ways of inner cultivation and outward action inform one another; through the essentials one nourishes the foundation, and the work proceeds uninterrupted from beginning to end. Apart from this, there is nothing to discuss concerning the way of learning.

Moreover, the learning of emperors and kings differs from that of commoners clad in plain cloth. Order and disorder depend upon the subtle workings of this mind: the critical point at which thoughts are held firm or let loose, and the ease with which one's bearing changes, are deeply to be feared. The transmission of rule from one emperor or king to another was recorded and became the Classics. Within these records, the learning of the mind originated in the succession of the Three Sages. Tang of Shang received it through knowledge gained by hearing of them. In his time, men such as Yi Yin and Lai Zhu assisted him, and worthy and sagely rulers arose in succession afterward. When it came to King Wen's reverent restraint and King Wu's care for virtue, men such as the Dukes of Zhou and Shao likewise assisted them. The chapter Against Luxurious Ease and the statement that the will is brought to tranquility through the Way [?] elucidate the subtleties of the learning of the mind and provide the foundation for establishing government and employing men. Rulers never tired of these teachings, nor did ministers find them burdensome.

In later ages, the transmission of the learning of the mind was sometimes manifest and sometimes obscure; order and disorder, survival and destruction varied accordingly. Thus these matters too were recorded and became histories. Histories are indeed the wings that support the Classics, and both are the field in which the learning of the mind is pursued. 所言其槩者耳心學精微之妙彼未悉也
夫幾康之與顧諟異用而同功學古之與
資人一事而互發今所謂尚書者固在也
孰非為心學而設乎試求其所謂心非所
謂惟危惟微者乎非所謂懋敬建中者乎
求其所謂學則又孰非弼直臣隣而古訓

translation_en:
…what he said was merely an outline; he did not fully comprehend the subtle profundities of the learning of the mind.

Attending to the incipient stirrings of affairs and to repose [?], and keeping one’s gaze upon Heaven’s luminous mandate, differ in application but achieve the same result. Studying antiquity and drawing upon others are a single undertaking whose aspects illuminate one another. The Book of Documents is certainly available to us today: what in it was not established for the learning of the mind? Examine what it calls the mind: is this not what it describes as precarious and subtle? Is it not what it describes as exerting oneself in reverence and establishing the mean? Examine what it calls learning: does this not everywhere involve assisting and correcting the ruler through ministers and close attendants, and drawing upon ancient teachings and established precedents? Looking at the classic as a whole, the meeting of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers declined into the ‘comprehensive employment of outstanding men’ [?]; at the culmination of this decline, Tang rose to power. The way of sincerity and trust declined into the casting aside of venerable elders; at the culmination of this decline, King Wu rose to power. Did this not depend upon the mind? Looking, moreover, at individual rulers, the Aheng upon whose corrective assistance the ruler still relied was the very one he had disobeyed; the red-slippered duke whom the ruler went out to welcome personally in the suburbs was the very one who had dwelt in the east; and the white-haired elder whom the ruler consulted about his plans was the very Jian Shu he had dismissed as decrepit. More striking still, Bo Jiong was still in office, yet the ruler had already fallen into excess over chariots and horses. Are not such extraordinary changes within a single mind profoundly alarming? The consequences of good and evil are thus very evident, while the principles of stimulus and response are exceedingly subtle. What Zhongsu described as being discussed most extensively, and as something whose underlying intent should be emulated—could this really be insufficient to encompass the affairs of emperors and kings?

Only those who fully master the learning of emperors and kings and grasp its meaning can set forth their Way; those who set forth its meaning can serve as models. The Mirror of the Tang is certainly available to us today. It has not yet…

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
之正史則已愚何敢因執事之言而兩重
於經邪雖然祖禹則有見矣嘗取其書而
讀之其所謂興廢治亂之由顯不可揜者
何莫而非人主之一心以見於君臣相與
之際乎故合而觀其一代太宗虛己則王
魏用而治一變而亂義府之徒出矣其極
也玄宗懲之則姚宋用而治既變而亂一
升一降以至於終若是而曰非心為之乎
又擇而觀其一君則碑表未立而征遼之
===
事已行金鑑方進而曲江之位已去奉天
方解而忠州之命已降一人之心前後懸
異而治亂亦因之夫一代之事可鑒則紹
復纘承之責不可辭一人之事可鑒則習
尚移奪之微不可忽而君子小人之治亂
有不容於揜者要其極則此心少變而小
人窺測已在其旁若夫君子之来則此心
既純而又必其意氣之孚契有以感召之
不然彼有見幾而作耳此則祖禹之深意

punctuated: 之正史則已，愚何敢因執事之言而兩重於經邪？雖然，祖禹則有見矣。嘗取其書而讀之，其所謂興廢治亂之由，顯不可揜者，何莫而非人主之一心以見於君臣相與之際乎？故合而觀其一代，太宗虛己，則王魏用而治；一變而亂，義府之徒出矣。其極也，玄宗懲之，則姚宋用而治；既變而亂，一升一降，以至於終。若是而曰非心為之乎？又擇而觀其一君，則碑表未立，而征遼之事已行；金鑑方進，而曲江之位已去；奉天方解，而忠州之命已降。一人之心，前後懸異，而治亂亦因之。夫一代之事可鑒，則紹復纘承之責不可辭；一人之事可鑒，則習尚移奪之微不可忽。而君子小人之治亂，有不容於揜者。要其極，則此心少變，而小人窺測已在其旁。若夫君子之来，則此心既純，而又必其意氣之孚契有以感召之。不然，彼有見幾而作耳。此則祖禹之深意
translation_en:
…the standard histories, then let that suffice [?]. How would I dare, on the strength of your words, to give both equal weight with the Classics? Nevertheless, Zuyu did have insight. I once took up his book and read it. What he calls the causes of rise and fall, order and disorder—so evident that they cannot be concealed—are they not all the ruler’s single heart manifesting itself in the dealings between sovereign and ministers? Thus, viewing the dynasty as a whole, when Taizong humbled himself, Wang Gui and Wei Zheng were employed, and order prevailed. Once this changed, disorder followed, and men such as Li Yifu emerged. When matters reached their worst, Xuanzong took warning: Yao Chong and Song Jing were employed, and order prevailed. Once this in turn changed, disorder followed. So it rose and fell until the dynasty’s end. Given this, could one say that the heart was not responsible?

Again, examining individual rulers, before the commemorative stele had been erected, the expedition against Liaodong was already under way; the Golden Mirror had only just been presented when Qujiang had already lost his post; the siege of Fengtian had only just been lifted when the order sending the minister to Zhongzhou had already been issued. The heart of a single man differed vastly from one moment to another, and order and disorder followed accordingly. If the affairs of a dynasty can serve as a mirror, the responsibility to continue, restore, and carry forward its legacy cannot be declined. If the affairs of an individual ruler can serve as a mirror, the subtle ways in which habitual inclinations shift and displace his resolve cannot be neglected. Nor can the order brought by exemplary men and the disorder brought by petty men be concealed. Ultimately, the slightest change in this heart finds petty men already at its side, watching and probing. As for attracting exemplary men, this heart must first be pure; moreover, there must be a genuine accord of purpose and spirit capable of drawing them to it. Otherwise, they will simply discern the first signs and act accordingly. This, then, was Zuyu’s deeper intention…

而有望於當時者。雖然，此亦尚書之意，而蔡沈所謂本於心者也；亦仲素之意，所謂變故最盛而當師其迹者。是誠可以佐於經，而有益於人主之學矣。
今日緝熙之功，固非草茅所敢知者。然竊見夫詔令之溫醇，法度之振起，大臣敬矣，而經筵之講頻仍；小民安矣，而當宁之懷隱惻。蓋愚所謂養康顧諟之功、學古資人之事，有不俟于言者。野人之獻，杞人之憂，竊欲就執事者質之。夫帝王之心學，非淺近之可言也。養之患其不充，持之患其不久。昔虞廷之謨，儆戒無虞；大禹之聖，不自滿假。雖以唐臣，亦或有十漸之說，以虞其未然者。小康之治，無所容議，而謨訓之敷陳，則亦今日公卿在位者之責也。愚何足以知之？
第四問
translation_en:
…and what he hoped for in his own time. Yet this is also the purport of the Book of Documents, what Cai Shen called “taking the mind as the foundation.” It is also Zhongsu’s meaning when he said that changes and upheavals were most abundant and that their traces should serve as our teachers. This can indeed supplement the Classics and benefit the ruler’s learning.
The present work of continually advancing in luminous virtue is certainly beyond what someone dwelling among the common people dares claim to understand. Yet I observe the warmth and generosity of the imperial edicts and the reinvigoration of laws and institutions. The great ministers are reverent, yet lectures at the Classics Colloquium continue frequently; the common people are at peace, yet His Majesty’s heart remains deeply solicitous. Thus the efforts I have spoken of—cultivating well-being and keeping Heaven’s mandate constantly in view—and the practices of learning from antiquity and drawing upon others need no further words. Still, with a rustic’s humble offering and the anxieties of the man of Qi who feared the sky would fall, I venture to submit these thoughts to you officials for examination. The learning of emperors and kings concerning the mind cannot be discussed in shallow or superficial terms. In nurturing it, one fears that it may not become full; in maintaining it, one fears that it may not endure. Long ago, the counsels at Shun’s court urged vigilance even when there was no cause for anxiety; sage though Great Yu was, he did not consider himself fully accomplished. Even among the ministers of the Tang, there was one who set forth the “Ten Gradual Changes,” anticipating dangers before they arose. Under the present government of modest peace and prosperity, there is no room for criticism; nevertheless, setting forth counsels and admonitions remains the responsibility of the dukes, ministers, and other officials now in office. How could an ignorant man like me presume to understand such matters?
Fourth Question

崔銑
同考試官主事劉　批〔此卷前二試俱超然〕
茂好而惓惓忠讜之懷復於末試發之如此
篇者非其平素究養完粹則倉皇對談之間
安能有是議論錄之諸餘具見矣然則子可
不謂天下士乎雖然二司之知子者文焉耳
而莫所以望於子者盖自有在其益圖之
同考試官編修李　批〔此卷五篇抑揚開闔〕
論不凡而此篇拈出張韓兩公學業以爲
同考試官編修賈　批〔篇篇筆勢滔滔文〕
辭例充其種種錄之
===
〔遶〕篇篇而此篇獨以見者二字爲矣大任重
之地充爲曹詩且皆是霸人而處分不差末
復律以聖賢之學子之養可槩知已
同考試官左中允傅　批〔張韓二公有宋〕
一代名臣其爲此論盖得之心而發于言者
子能知之又直推至三代以上聖賢事業以
爲準的亦可謂有定見矣願觀臨事之定力
punctuated:
崔銑

同考試官主事劉批：「此卷前二試俱超然茂好，而惓惓忠藎之懷，復於末試發之如此。策者非其平素充養完粹，則倉皇對談之間，安能有是議論？錄之，諸餘具見矣。然則予可不謂天下士乎？雖然，有司之知子者文焉耳，而其所以望於子者，固自有在。甚至圖之。」

同考試官編修李批：「此卷五策，抑揚開闔，議論不凡，而此策拈出張、韓兩公學業以為斷例，尤見擅場，敬錄之。」

同考試官編修賈批：「策藳筆勢滔滔，文思稱義，而此篇獨以見素二字為受大任重之地，尤為竒特。且敘忠肅人品，處分不差，末復律以聖賢之學，子之養可槩知已。」

同考試官左中允傅批：「張、韓二公，有宋一代名臣，其為此論，蓋得之心而發于言者。子能知之，又直推至三代以上聖賢事業以為準的，亦可謂有定見矣。願觀臨事之定力
translation_en:
Cui Xian

Associate Examiner Liu, a Secretary, comments: “This candidate’s work in the first two sessions was outstanding and richly accomplished; his earnest devotion and loyalty find expression once again in this policy essay from the final session. Had the essayist not habitually cultivated himself to fullness, integrity, and purity, how could he produce such arguments amid the haste of answering? By recording this essay, we reveal all his other qualities as well. Could I, then, not be called a scholar of the realm? [?] Nevertheless, what we officials know of you comes only through your writing; what we hope for from you certainly extends further. Give this the utmost consideration [?].”

Associate Examiner Li, a Compiler, comments: “The five policy essays in this script show skill in emphasis and restraint, opening out and drawing together; their arguments are exceptional. This essay, in particular, singles out the learning and accomplishments of the two gentlemen Zhang and Han as precedents for judgment, displaying especial mastery. I respectfully record it.”

Associate Examiner Jia, a Compiler, comments: “The policy-essay drafts flow with a surging energy of the brush, and their literary conception accords with their meaning. This essay alone takes the two characters ‘manifesting simplicity’ as the foundation for assuming great and weighty responsibilities [?], an especially remarkable approach. Moreover, its account of the character of the gentleman posthumously titled Zhongsu is discriminating and accurate. At the end, it again measures him against the learning of the sages and worthies. From this, one can broadly discern the cultivation you have attained.”

Associate Examiner Fu, Left Associate Advisor, comments: “The two gentlemen Zhang and Han were eminent ministers of the Song dynasty. In making this argument, they surely expressed in words what they had grasped in their hearts. You understand this and, moreover, trace matters directly back to the undertakings of the sages and worthies of the Three Dynasties and earlier, taking these as your standard. You may indeed be said to possess settled convictions. I hope to observe your steadfastness when confronted with affairs …

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
於他日拭目以俟
考試官學士楊批淵博之才英毅之氣
宏遠之識具於文字中見之惜得卷之晚不
能盡錄其文耳意子之所欲自見者當不止
此也願勗之以不負今日之選
考試官學士張批此卷前二場知子為留
心理學者末場五答尤見有用抱負此問本以
試諸士子心術子則何待此問然即此答足以
驗持養之有素矣
===
有天下之定見有天下之定力然後可與
處天下之大事矣定見者何智是也定力
者何膽是也智非權譎縱橫之謂也理明
於心而事有定見膽非剛暴麤悍之謂也
氣充於體而事有定力是非利害錯雜無
端而智以料之亦足以驗吾好學之功死
生禍福轉盼莫測而氣以決之亦足以資
吾善道之本愚叨承執事之問而有槩於
心矣張忠定公有曰大小之事皆須用智

吾吾道之本愚叨承執事之問而有槩於

punctuated:
於他日，拭目以俟。

考試官學士楊批：淵博之才、英毅之氣、宏遠之識，具於文字中見之。惜得卷之晚，不能盡錄其文耳。意子之所欲自見者，當不止此也。願勗之，以不負今日之選。

考試官學士張批：此卷前二場，知子為留心理學者；末場五答，尤見有用抱負。此問本以試諸士子心術，子則何待此問？然即此答，足以驗持養之有素矣。

有天下之定見，有天下之定力，然後可與處天下之大事矣。定見者何？智是也。定力者何？膽是也。智非權譎縱橫之謂也，理明於心，而事有定見；膽非剛暴麤悍之謂也，氣充於體，而事有定力。是非利害錯雜無端，而智以料之，亦足以驗吾好學之功；死生禍福轉盼莫測，而氣以決之，亦足以資吾善道之本。愚叨承執事之問，而有槩於心矣。張忠定公有曰：「大小之事，皆須用智。」
translation_en:
…in the days to come; I await it eagerly.

Comment by Examiner Yang, Academician: Your profound learning and talent, your spirited resolve, and your broad and far-reaching understanding are all evident in your writing. I regret only that I received this script so late that I could not include all its compositions. I imagine that what you wish to reveal of yourself surely extends beyond this. I hope you will strive onward, so as to live up to your selection today.

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Academician: From the first two sessions represented in this script, I can tell that you devote yourself to the study of principle. Your five answers in the final session reveal particularly clearly your aspirations for practical service. This question was originally intended to test the candidates’ moral dispositions. What need had you of such a question? Nevertheless, this answer alone suffices to demonstrate your longstanding cultivation and preservation of the mind.

Only when a man possesses firm judgment concerning the affairs of the realm and the resolve to act upon it can he be entrusted with handling the realm’s great affairs. What is firm judgment? It is wisdom. What is steadfast resolve? It is courage. Wisdom does not mean cunning expedients and political maneuvering: when principle is clear in the mind, one has firm judgment in dealing with affairs. Courage does not mean violent obstinacy or coarse ferocity: when vital energy fills the body, one has steadfast resolve in dealing with affairs. When right and wrong, benefit and harm are tangled together without any discernible order, using wisdom to assess them also suffices to verify the fruits of my devotion to learning. When death and life, calamity and good fortune shift unpredictably in the blink of an eye, drawing upon vital energy to decide how to act also suffices to strengthen the foundation of my pursuit of the good Way. Having had the undeserved honor of receiving your question, I, in my ignorance, have formed a general understanding in my mind. Lord Zhang Zhongding once said: “In affairs both great and small, one must always employ wisdom.” …

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
韓忠獻公有曰成大事者在膽夫豈不義
而二公言之蓋必反觀於心而有得屢試
於事而輒效用之於外而郡國治用之於
內而朝廷安是宜我朱子錄之以為後
人法也愚請先以聖賢之所論試言之可
乎孔子曰知者不惑勇者不懼朱子以為
知足以明理故不惑勇足以配道義故不
懼孟子曰我知言我善養吾浩然之氣朱
子以為知言則有以明夫道義而於天下
===
之事無所疑養氣則有以配夫道義而於
天下之事無所懼是知也知言也非忠定
之所謂智者乎勇也養氣也非忠獻之所
謂膽者乎又嘗即聖人之所行者而論之
吾夫子仕魯之時三卿皆連都邑及陪臣
之叛也則乘機而勸以墮之當是時并兼
攘奪蓋駸駸乎其分魯矣從容數語天理
自動累世積弊一朝以除非辨別之智有
以深感其心吾不知日長月益在列之臣

punctuated: 韓忠獻公有曰：「成大事者在膽。」夫豈不義而二公言之？蓋必反觀於心而有得，屢試於事而輒效，用之於外而郡國治，用之於內而朝廷安，是宜我朱子錄之以為後人法也。愚請先以聖賢之所論試言之，可乎？孔子曰：「知者不惑，勇者不懼。」朱子以為知足以明理，故不惑；勇足以配道義，故不懼。孟子曰：「我知言，我善養吾浩然之氣。」朱子以為知言則有以明夫道義，而於天下之事無所疑；養氣則有以配夫道義，而於天下之事無所懼。是知也，知言也，非忠定之所謂智者乎？勇也，養氣也，非忠獻之所謂膽者乎？又嘗即聖人之所行者而論之。吾夫子仕魯之時，三卿皆連都邑，及陪臣之叛也，則乘機而勸以墮之。當是時，并兼攘奪，蓋駸駸乎其分魯矣。從容數語，天理自動，累世積弊，一朝以除。非辨別之智有以深感其心，吾不知日長月益，在列之臣
translation_en:
…Lord Han Zhongxian said, “Accomplishing great affairs depends on courage.” Could this be contrary to righteousness, yet still have been said by these two gentlemen? Surely they reflected inwardly and gained an understanding, repeatedly tested it in affairs and invariably found it effective. Applied outside the capital, it brought good government to the prefectures and domains; applied within, it brought peace to the imperial court. It was therefore fitting that our Master Zhu recorded their words as a model for later generations. May I first attempt to explain this through the teachings of the sages and worthies?

Confucius said, “The wise are not perplexed; the courageous are not afraid.” Master Zhu held that wisdom suffices to illuminate principle, and thus prevents perplexity; courage suffices to accord with the Way and righteousness, and thus prevents fear. Mencius said, “I understand words, and I am good at nourishing my vast, flowing vital energy.” Master Zhu held that understanding words enables one to comprehend the Way and righteousness, leaving no doubts concerning the affairs of the world; nourishing one’s vital energy enables one to accord with the Way and righteousness, leaving no fear concerning the affairs of the world. Are this wisdom and this understanding of words not what Zhongding meant by “wisdom”? Are this courage and this nourishment of vital energy not what Zhongxian meant by “courage”?

Let us also consider what the sage actually did. When our Master served in Lu, the three ministers all held interconnected fortified towns [?]. When their retainers rebelled, he seized the opportunity to urge the ministers to dismantle those towns. At that time, through annexation and seizure, they were rapidly approaching the partition of Lu. With a few calmly spoken words, Heaven’s principle stirred of itself, and abuses accumulated over generations were eliminated in a single morning. Had his discerning wisdom not profoundly moved their hearts, I do not know, as these abuses grew day by day and month by month, how the ministers in office …

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
何以處之夾谷之會兩君各就壇坫及萊
人之劫也則據禮而責以卻之當是時凌
逼干擬盖岌岌乎其無魯矣慷慨數言凶
威自歛數年侵地一旦以歸非義理之勇
有以深折其心吾不知干盟倡好在行之
臣何以待之大禹之治水也八年過門之
前雖其父鯀不試而自寬而九河之疏行
所無事非處大智者能之事周公之相國
也三叔流言之後雖其君亦不能以不疑
===
而碩膚之遜處以無事非有定力者能之
乎嗚呼此皆大聖人所為所以當大事成
大功而盡善盡美者也則夫陳平晁錯趙
雲姜維之數子者其人品之高下事功之
成敗又何必屑屑然為執事道哉若夫二
公之所處則亦有可得而言者矣忠定之
治蜀也用心鎮撫人以大和其為此言盖
己所嘗用者宋景文公曰姿宇爽邁謀謨
沈敏總物纖密絕人遠甚而韓忠獻公亦

punctuated:
何以處之？夾谷之會，兩君各就壇坫，及萊人之劫也，則據禮而責以卻之。當是時，凌逼干擬，盖岌岌乎其無魯矣。慷慨數言，凶威自歛，數年侵地，一旦以歸。非義理之勇有以深折其心，吾不知干盟倡好，在行之臣何以待之？大禹之治水也，八年過門之前，雖其父鯀不試而自寬，而九河之疏，行所無事，非處大智者能之事。周公之相國也，三叔流言之後，雖其君亦不能以不疑，而碩膚之遜，處以無事，非有定力者能之乎？嗚呼！此皆大聖人所為，所以當大事、成大功而盡善盡美者也。則夫陳平、晁錯、趙雲、姜維之數子者，其人品之高下、事功之成敗，又何必屑屑然為執事道哉？

若夫二公之所處，則亦有可得而言者矣。忠定之治蜀也，用心鎮撫，人以大和。其為此言，盖己所嘗用者。宋景文公曰：「姿宇爽邁，謀謨沈敏，總物纖密，絕人遠甚。」而韓忠獻公亦
translation_en:
…how could they have dealt with it? At the meeting at Jiagu, the two rulers each took their places on the ceremonial platform. When the men of Lai attempted to seize them, Confucius invoked ritual propriety to rebuke and repel them. At that moment, intimidation and encroachment [?] had brought Lu perilously close to extinction. With a few impassioned words, he caused their savage aggression to subside; territory seized over several years was restored in a single day. Had his courage, grounded in moral principle, not profoundly subdued their hearts, I do not know how the ministers accompanying the ruler to seek a covenant and establish friendly relations could have met the situation. When Great Yu controlled the floods, during the eight years when he passed his own gate, although his father Gun had failed, he remained at ease [?]; in dredging the Nine Rivers, he proceeded without forcing matters. This was a task requiring great wisdom [?]. When the Duke of Zhou served as chief minister, after the Three Uncles spread their rumors, even his ruler could not avoid suspecting him. Yet he modestly yielded credit for his great achievements and met the situation without agitation. Could anyone without steadfast resolve have done this? Alas! These were all deeds of great sages: through them they faced great affairs and accomplished great achievements with consummate goodness and perfection. As for Chen Ping, Chao Cuo, Zhao Yun, and Jiang Wei, why need I trouble you, honored examiners, with minute accounts of the relative heights of their character or the success and failure of their achievements?

As for how the two lords handled their circumstances, there is also something that can be said. When Lord Zhongding governed Shu, he devoted himself to pacifying and reassuring the people, bringing them into great harmony. His statement thus concerned something he himself had put into practice. Lord Song Jingwen said: “His bearing was bright and unconstrained; his planning, profound and perceptive; his management of affairs, meticulous and thorough. He surpassed others by a very great distance.” And Lord Han Zhongxian also …

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
曰以魁奇豪傑之才逢時自奮智畧神出
勳業赫赫震暴當世誠一世偉人也嗚呼
是豈可以凡士目之乎忠獻之作相也悉
力調和國以大定其為此言盖身所甞試
者王文公曰毁譽幾至於萬端夷險常持
於一意為古人所未甞任大臣所不敢而
歐陽文忠公亦曰臨大事决大議不動聲
氣而措天下於泰山之安可謂社稷之臣
矣嗚呼是豈可以常材目之乎二公所為
===
雖於聖賢之學未敢謂深有所得而欲謂
其皆無所見而任性以行之又豈敢哉觀
忠定以不學無術警萊公則忠定固未甞
不學者也忠獻以毋廢讀書勉荆公則忠
獻固未甞不學者也但不能真積力久深
求逺造學問之所得有限量故功業之所
就有分數然學與不學之間乃邪正善惡
之所由分上達下達間不容髮不可以不
慮也學之於無事之時則精義入神直養

求遠造學問之所得有限量故功業之所
就有分數然學與不學之間乃邪正善惡
之所由分上達下達間不容髮不可以下
慮也學之於無事之時則精義入神直□
punctuated: 曰：「以魁奇豪傑之才，逢時自奮，智畧神出，勳業赫赫，震暴當世，誠一世偉人也。」嗚呼！是豈可以凡士目之乎？忠獻之作相也，悉力調和，國以大定。其為此言，盖身所甞試者。王文公曰：「毁譽幾至於萬端，夷險常持於一意，為古人所未甞，任大臣所不敢。」而歐陽文忠公亦曰：「臨大事，决大議，不動聲氣，而措天下於泰山之安，可謂社稷之臣矣。」嗚呼！是豈可以常材目之乎？二公所為，雖於聖賢之學未敢謂深有所得，而欲謂其皆無所見而任性以行之，又豈敢哉？觀忠定以不學無術警萊公，則忠定固未甞不學者也；忠獻以毋廢讀書勉荆公，則忠獻固未甞不學者也。但不能真積力久，深求逺造，學問之所得有限量，故功業之所就有分數。然學與不學之間，乃邪正善惡之所由分，上達下達，間不容髮，不可以不慮也。學之於無事之時，則精義入神，直養
translation_en:
…said: “With extraordinary and heroic talents, he met his opportunity and rose by his own exertions. His wisdom and strategy emerged with uncanny brilliance; his achievements were illustrious, shaking his age with their force [?]. He was truly a great man of his generation.” Ah! How could one regard him as an ordinary scholar? When Zhongxian served as chief councilor, he devoted all his strength to fostering harmony, and the state thereby attained great stability. These words of his surely arose from what he had personally put to the test. Wang Wengong said: “Though praise and blame took almost ten thousand forms, in ease and peril he remained constant in a single purpose. He did what men of antiquity had never done and undertook what great ministers did not dare.” Ouyang Wenzhong likewise said: “Confronting great affairs and deciding great deliberations, without any change in voice or countenance he placed the realm in security as firm as Mount Tai. He may indeed be called a minister who safeguards the altars of soil and grain.” Ah! How could one regard him as a man of ordinary ability?

Although I would not venture to claim that these two lords’ actions reflected a profound understanding of the learning of the sages and worthies, how could I dare to say that neither had any insight and that they acted merely according to their natural dispositions? Consider how Zhongding warned Lord Lai against being without learning or practical competence: Zhongding himself certainly was not without learning. Zhongxian urged Lord Jing never to abandon reading: Zhongxian himself certainly was not without learning. Yet they could not truly accumulate understanding through sustained effort, investigate deeply, and attain far-reaching mastery. Their gains in learning were limited, and so their achievements were correspondingly bounded. Nevertheless, the distinction between learning and not learning is precisely where deviation and rectitude, goodness and evil, diverge. Between advancing toward higher understanding and descending toward lower pursuits, there is not room for a hair’s breadth: this demands reflection. If one studies in times free from affairs, one refines one’s understanding of principles until it penetrates the numinous, and nourishes oneself through uprightness…

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
無害而有以立其體用之於有事之日則
先覺是賢大勇無敵而有以達諸用過此
以往則古昔名臣之績皆可企及而於聖
賢之事亦可馴致矣然用智如水不防則
潰决而不能止任氣如火不戢則焚燎而
莫可救一則或流於詐而不知正一則或
源於縱而不知法萬一忽於學問而徒任
血氣則平居也擇之不精倉卒也發之不
中滑稽圓轉者動以忠定相方專愎放肆
===
者又以忠獻自擬幾何不踰大閑取敗闕
而墮於小人之歸也哉此則愚生之所未
能無疑而執事明問固所深慮者也愚也
輒述舊聞以復若夫所謂受大任重之地
云者固非末學所敢承也幸進而教之
第五問
安磐
同考試官郎中周批
〔對策以知故實為難而尤以能區處時事為貴此卷五策援古證〕

同考試官郎中周　批〔策以知故實爲難〕
〔而尤以能慮時事爲貴此卷五策據　論〕
punctuated:
無害，而有以立其體；用之於有事之日，則先覺是賢，大勇無敵，而有以達諸用。過此以往，則古昔名臣之績皆可企及，而於聖賢之事亦可馴致矣。然用智如水，不防則潰决而不能止；任氣如火，不戢則焚燎而莫可救。一則或流於詐而不知正，一則或源於縱而不知法。萬一忽於學問而徒任血氣，則平居也擇之不精，倉卒也發之不中。滑稽圓轉者動以忠定相方，專愎放肆者又以忠獻自擬，幾何不踰大閑、取敗闕，而墮於小人之歸也哉？此則愚生之所未能無疑，而執事明問固所深慮者也。愚也輒述舊聞以復。若夫所謂受大任重之地云者，固非末學所敢承也。幸進而教之。
第五問
安磐
同考試官郎中周批
〔對策以知故實為難，而尤以能區處時事為貴。此卷五策援古證〕
translation_en:
…without harm, thereby establishing its fundamental substance. When this learning is put into practice as affairs arise, prior understanding is prized, great courage is invincible, and its practical applications can thus be fully realized. Advancing beyond this, one may hope to equal the achievements of eminent ministers of antiquity and gradually attain even the accomplishments of sages and worthies. Yet the exercise of intelligence resembles water: unless contained, it breaches its banks and cannot be stopped. Giving rein to one's spirit resembles fire: unless restrained, it blazes up beyond remedy. The one may lapse into deceit, losing sight of rectitude; the other may spring from self-indulgence, losing sight of proper rules. Should one neglect learning and rely solely on one's impulses, one's choices in ordinary times will lack discernment, and one's responses in emergencies will miss the mark. Glib and accommodating men constantly compare themselves to Zhongding, while obstinate and unrestrained men liken themselves to Zhongxian. How could they avoid transgressing the great moral boundaries, bringing failure and fault upon themselves, and ending up among petty men? This is what I, your foolish student, cannot help but have doubts about, and it is surely the profound concern underlying your discerning question. I have ventured to recount what I previously learned in reply. As for your words about occupying a position entrusted with great responsibilities and heavy burdens, that is assuredly something I, a novice in learning, dare not accept. I hope you will offer me further instruction.
Fifth Question
An Pan 安磐

〔In answering policy questions, knowledge of historical precedents is difficult to achieve; still more valuable is the ability to deal effectively with current affairs. The five policy essays in this script invoke antiquity to substantiate…〕

text:

…the underlying principles; his talent and spirit are outstanding. The policy essay on frontier defense, in particular, addresses a matter of the greatest urgency. Its answers to the individual points are more detailed, and at the end it again cites essential words of Kaoting (Zhu Xi) to settle the argument. This is indeed an incontrovertible judgment. It should not be treated as an instance of the commonplace talk of Confucian scholars. It deserves first place among the Spring and Autumn Annals candidates.

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
不善則無以適通變之宜周于法而善其
用此講邉備者之所當知也執事策試諸
生以邉備四事為問迂愚不足以語此然
縹緗鉛槧之餘竊有江湖
廟堂之念久矣敢不敬陳所聞者以復選將
也治兵也屯田也馬政也皆邉備之大者
在
祖宗朝自有畫一之法雖行之萬世可也而執
事顧復致疑於其間毋乃法之未善乎抑
===
亦用之者之過也蓋今之選將也有會薦
之舊條有武舉之新格其法亦云備矣獨
意其擇之不精而馭之未盡也擇之不精
者弓馬記誦之不足以得之也謂宜教之
也必先以諸家之兵法歷代之史傳使博
觀古今成敗之迹試之也必參以天下之
夷情職方之圖本使備知地形風土之宜
於是嘗之以治兵寄之以邉障日養其望
以至于大受而異才庶幾乎可得也馭之

===

之舊條有武舉之新格莫謂亦云備矣犹
意其擇之不精而馭之未盡也擇之不精
者予嘗記誦之不足以得之也謂宜教之
而必先以諸家之兵法歷代之史傳使博

於是嘗之以治兵督之以邊障日養其望

punctuated: 不善，則無以適通變之宜。周于法而善其用，此講邉備者之所當知也。執事策試諸生，以邉備四事為問。迂愚不足以語此，然縹緗鉛槧之餘，竊有江湖廟堂之念久矣，敢不敬陳所聞者以復？選將也，治兵也，屯田也，馬政也，皆邉備之大者。在祖宗朝，自有畫一之法，雖行之萬世可也。而執事顧復致疑於其間，毋乃法之未善乎？抑亦用之者之過也？蓋今之選將也，有會薦之舊條，有武舉之新格，其法亦云備矣。獨意其擇之不精，而馭之未盡也。擇之不精者，弓馬記誦之不足以得之也。謂宜教之也，必先以諸家之兵法、歷代之史傳，使博觀古今成敗之迹；試之也，必參以天下之夷情、職方之圖本，使備知地形風土之宜。於是嘗之以治兵，寄之以邉障，日養其望，以至于大受，而異才庶幾乎可得也。馭之
translation_en:
…if their application is poor, there is no way to respond appropriately to changing circumstances. To make the regulations comprehensive and apply them well: this is what those who discuss frontier defense ought to understand. You, sir, have tested the candidates with policy questions concerning four matters of frontier defense. Unworldly and ignorant as I am, I am unequal to discussing these things. Yet, in the intervals of reading and writing, I have long harbored concern for the court even while living far from it. How could I fail respectfully to set forth what I have heard in reply?

Selecting commanders, training troops, military agricultural colonies, and horse administration are all major matters of frontier defense. Under our imperial ancestors, there were already uniform regulations that could have remained in force for ten thousand generations. Yet you, sir, have raised doubts about them once again. Could it be that the regulations are inadequate? Or is the fault with those who apply them?

For selecting commanders today, there are the old provisions for joint recommendation and the new regulations for the military examinations. The rules may indeed be called comprehensive. I suspect only that selection is insufficiently discriminating and that the management of those selected is imperfect. Selection is insufficiently discriminating because archery, horsemanship, memorization, and recitation do not suffice to identify the right men. I would suggest that their instruction must begin with the military treatises of the various masters and the histories and biographies of successive dynasties, so that they may survey widely the records of success and failure, past and present. Their examinations must also incorporate information about non-Chinese peoples throughout the realm and maps held by the Bureau of Operations, so that they may gain a thorough understanding of terrain and local conditions. Then let them be tried in training troops and entrusted with frontier defenses, steadily fostering their standing until they can assume great responsibilities. In this way, exceptional talent may perhaps be found. As for the management of these men…

title: 弘治十八年會試錄
text:
未盡者居間則約束之太嚴僨事則寬假
之太過也謂宜重邊守之寄而厚其賞專
閫外之權而久其任監軍文吏皆不得為
之牽制一有僨事則或輕或重一議之以
軍法而不得遷就於末減之例可也治兵
之法則編戍之籍有定招募之令無時往
歲嘗募之京師矣或謂是多市井之無賴
與其收之於無賴孰若撫之於見伍寬其
工役禁之尅剥放厚其犒賞之資養其果銳
===
之氣則在營者皆勝兵也近歲又嘗募之
畿右矣而或謂是多他郡之白籍與其收
之於白籍孰若用之於土兵給以閒田蠲
其徭役二十而為兵五十而免籍則餘夫
亦可募也以屯田言之衛所之設多在州
縣之後民田多膏腴屯田多瘠鹵歲月漸
深則視勤惰而為地利隨貧富而易地主
議者欲從而覈之覈之誠是也然命使不
能履畝而驗則必委之所司所司不肯原

軍法而不得遷就於末減之例可也治兵
之法則編戍之籍有定招募之令無時往

與其收之於無賴孰若撫之於見伍寬其
