之氣則在營者皆勝兵近歲又嘗募之
㕓右矣或謂是多佃戶之白籍與其收

議者欲從而聚之聚之誠是也然命使不

punctuated:
未盡者，居間則約束之太嚴，僨事則寬假之太過也。謂宜重邊守之寄而厚其賞，專閫外之權而久其任，監軍文吏皆不得為之牽制。一有僨事，則或輕或重，一議之以軍法，而不得遷就於末減之例，可也。

治兵之法，則編戍之籍有定，招募之令無時。往歲嘗募之京師矣，或謂是多市井之無賴。與其收之於無賴，孰若撫之於見伍？寬其工役，禁之尅剥，放厚其犒賞之資，養其果銳之氣，則在營者皆勝兵也。近歲又嘗募之畿右矣，而或謂是多他郡之白籍。與其收之於白籍，孰若用之於土兵？給以閒田，蠲其徭役，二十而為兵，五十而免籍，則餘夫亦可募也。

以屯田言之，衛所之設，多在州縣之後。民田多膏腴，屯田多瘠鹵。歲月漸深，則視勤惰而為地利，隨貧富而易地主。議者欲從而覈之，覈之誠是也。然命使不能履畝而驗，則必委之所司；所司不肯原
translation_en:
…As for the inadequacy of their management, in ordinary times [?] they are restrained too strictly, while when they fail in their duties they are treated with excessive leniency. I submit that responsibility for defending the frontier should be given greater weight and rewarded generously. Commanders should have sole authority over military operations beyond the gates and remain long in office; neither army supervisors nor civil officials should be allowed to hamper them. Whenever they fail in their duties, the case, whether minor or serious, should be judged entirely under military law, without accommodating them through precedents for reducing punishment.

As for the methods of managing troops, the registers of men assigned to garrison duty are fixed, but recruitment orders are issued at no fixed intervals. In past years men were recruited in the capital, but some said that these were mostly idlers from the streets and marketplaces. Rather than enlist such idlers, would it not be better to care for the men already in the ranks? Lighten their labor duties, prohibit exploitation of them, increase [?] the funds for their rewards, and nurture their courage and fighting spirit: then all those in camp will be fit for combat. In recent years men were also recruited in the western part of the capital region, but some said that these were mostly people from other prefectures without regular household registration. Rather than enlist such people, would it not be better to employ local troops? Give them unused land and exempt them from labor services; let them become soldiers at twenty and be removed from the military registers at fifty. In this way, surplus adult males could also be recruited.

As for military agricultural colonies, the guards and battalions were mostly established after the prefectures and counties. Civilian fields are generally fertile, while military colony fields are generally barren and saline. As the years pass, the productivity of land comes to depend on diligence or neglect, and its ownership changes according to poverty or wealth. Those discussing the matter wish to investigate this situation. Investigation is certainly right. But if the commissioners appointed cannot walk the fields and inspect them, they must entrust the matter to the responsible authorities; if those authorities are unwilling to trace the origins…

translation_en:
…trace matters back to their beginnings, some may instead use this as grounds for accusations and litigation, even seeking to seize for themselves land on which others have securely pursued their livelihoods for a hundred or several tens of years. Officials turn this into a source of profit, and the people experience it as a scourge. Can one fail to be troubled by this?
The abuses in horse administration are especially severe. People entrusted with raising horses in the interior suffer from annual demands for compensation. New assessments are piled upon old arrears, while deaths and losses cause hardship in the issuing and replacement of horses [?]. Orders granting relief must therefore be issued from time to time. As for horses assigned to soldiers, men in the same squad likewise suffer from having to compensate for one another’s losses. Monthly allocations of fodder and beans serve only to supply private households, while annual revenues from pasturelands sometimes find their way into commanders’ coffers. The “stump-head” payments for lost horses must also be somewhat reduced. As for horses raised under official management in outlying prefectures, inquire into the herdsmen and their names remain on the registers, but the men are gone; inquire into the pasturelands and even their registers have been destroyed. Recently, a censor has been specially assigned to supervise these matters. Replacements for herdsmen who fled have already been selected, and concealed pasturelands have been investigated and recovered, restoring the former arrangements. Yet plans must also be made for their future care and lasting maintenance.
These four matters are all urgent tasks of frontier defense. What I have humbly presented concerns only correcting imbalances and remedying abuses; I have not yet reached the essential point. What is essential? It lies simply in the people employed. For people are the ones who put laws into practice. Everyone can speak of obtaining suitable people, but when it comes to actual administration, suitable people are not necessarily obtained for every post. Thus their…

translation_en: …abuses and imbalances have reached such a point that they cannot but trouble the court’s deliberations. Even so, there is something greater still. In the sages’ way of controlling the non-Chinese peoples, the foundation lies not in military might but in virtuous achievement; preparedness lies not at the frontiers but at court; and the means lie not in troops and provisions but in the governing order and discipline. These are the words of Master Zhu Xi, intended as counsel for those who govern all under Heaven throughout the ages. What is your judgment, sir?

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

All that the Six Classics contain consists of the methods by which the Two Emperors and Three Kings achieved good government. Confucius transmitted these to instruct later generations, hoping that posterity would attain the government of Tang Yao, Yu Shun, and the Three Dynasties. Yet commentators maintain that, since Confucius, the Six Classics have remained books never put to the test. Is this not because their Way has not been clearly understood?

Our Emperor Taizu Gao founded the great imperial enterprise and exalted classical learning to influence all regions. In his edict inaugurating the examinations, he spoke first of mastery of the Classics. Emperor Wen succeeded him, honoring and elucidating the Six Classics and promulgating them throughout the realm. Statements that contradicted the Classics and departed from the Way were almost entirely suppressed. Thereupon, scholars throughout the realm studied them from childhood, answered policy questions and passed the examinations, and went on to undertake official duties, devise plans, and offer proposals…

translation_en:
…in every action taking the Six Classics as their standard. The successive sage emperors continued this work, ever deepening its influence and refining its effects. As the Way endured and its transforming influence spread fully, their governance could indeed rival the flourishing rule of Tang Yao, Yu Shun, and the Three Dynasties. Among those who assisted and supported them, outstanding men renowned in their age followed one another in great numbers; all were scholars versed in the Classics. This is the demonstrated efficacy of the Six Classics.
Now, with our sagacious sovereign on the throne, the cultivation of scholars and selection of men follow established precedents in every respect. He once commanded his Confucian officials to compile the Collected Statutes of the Great Ming (Da Ming huidian), comprehensively recording the splendor of this dynasty’s institutions, complementing the Six Classics. Recently he further decreed the compilation of the Essential Compilation of the Comprehensive Mirror (Tongjian zuanyao) to support this endeavor, enabling scholars throughout the realm to gain broad knowledge of the events of antiquity and a clear understanding of the affairs of the present age, bringing both together in the study of the Classics. The Way of the Six Classics has thus become still more fully manifest throughout the realm, and Confucius…

translation_en:
…the achievement of his editing and transmitting has, at this point, once again found practical expression. Ah, how splendid! In the second month of the yichou year of Hongzhi [1505], the Ministry of Rites was due to conduct the Metropolitan Examination for scholars from throughout the realm. His Majesty commanded Academician Yuan zhen and me, Tinghe, his servants, to preside over it. We reverently received his gracious intent and worked diligently and cautiously. After twenty days, we reported the task completed. By imperial decision, three hundred successful candidates were selected, all well versed in the learning of the Six Classics.
These scholars understand the Classics, but how well they can put their learning to use in the world remains to be seen. To understand the Classics yet be unable to serve the world is merely the learning of conventional scholars. In the age of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, the Six Classics were not yet complete. We do not know what books their ministers read, yet their achievements were so…

之大。今人所讀誦，往往有前世之所未見者，而建立顧或不能無慊於古，亦獨何哉？繼自今，蜚英騰茂，為一世名臣，承先正已試之效而又進焉，以媲休唐虞三代之臣者，非諸士之責而誰與？臣濫竿試事，於諸士終身所至，不能無厚望焉者，故欲以是飭勵之，而因以附於試錄之後云。
奉議大夫、左春坊大學士兼翰林院侍讀學士楊廷和謹序。
translation_en:
…so great. What men today read and recite often includes things never seen by earlier generations; yet their accomplishments may still fall short of those of antiquity. Why should this be? From now onward, to win renown for excellence, become eminent ministers of their age, carry forward the proven achievements of former worthies and advance beyond them, thereby matching the glory of the ministers of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties—whose responsibility is this if not yours, gentlemen? Your servant has unworthily participated in conducting this examination [?], and cannot but entertain high hopes for what you gentlemen will achieve over your lifetimes. I therefore wish to admonish and encourage you with these words, and accordingly append them to the examination record.
Respectfully composed as a preface by Yang Tinghe, Grand Master for Court Discussion, Grand Secretary of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent [?], concurrently Academician Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy.
